19. Brunch Interlude

Summary for the Chapter:

Set between 2x19 and 2x20. The brunch we were promised and never got to see, plus more cute girlfriend stuff, because Goddamnit, There Needs To Be Some Happiness Before Everything Goes To Shit (Again). You don't really need to read this, because there's not really any plot, but it's cute and it's here, so...

 

The first thing Lena did, once the apartment door was opened for her, was pull Alex into a very careful hug. Alex, for her part in it, hugged back right away, and her laughter was more surprised than mocking.

“Hey, Legs.”

“Hey.”

“The floor’s there to take over if you get tired.”

Oh. Right.

Lena set Alex down sheepishly before being dragged into a second hug. “Good to see you.”

“You, too. I’m sorry I wasn’t - ”

“There were already too many cooks in the kitchen. Don’t worry about it.”

“I’ll give it my best shot.” 

Alex looked good. She looked alive. She was nursing some split knuckles and there was a bandage on her shoulder, but she wore it like an epaulette, like it was part of a dress uniform. Plus, as buried as Lena had been in, y’know, synthesizing an entire element, Kara had been just as busy playing anxious guard dog for her lovingly exasperated big sister.

“Speaking of, can you work some girlfriend magic and get her out of my hair?” Alex asked, grinning. “She’s decided that her new excuse for hanging around is organizing my shoes.”

“You have more than one pair of shoes?”

“Tac boots, heels, and sneakers. Only one of those has been replaced in the past year.”

“And it’s not available in stores.”

“Nope.” 

“I got it. Kara?”

“Lena!”

One of Alex’s two individual stilettos clattered to the floor. There was a whoosh, and then two strong arms around Lena’s shoulders, pulling her close. Lena got an involuntary but much welcomed whiff of Kara’s shampoo, and gave herself license to sink into that hug, wrapping her arms around Kara’s waist tight and burying her face in Kara’s shoulders. 

It had been, at most, a day and a half since she’d seen Kara last, but it felt like decades. Her work ethic went from obscene to absent around her girlfriend, more often than not, so it couldn’t really be helped, but Lena had never been so happy for the advent of the weekend than she was with an armful of Kryptonian.

“I’ve missed you.”

“Missed you, too. Now, c’mon, we have brunch to eat.”

“Is it the place with bottomless mimosas?”

“Bottomless waffles.”

Kara kissed Lena’s forehead. “Ooh! Thank Rao! I already cleaned out Alex’s kitchen.”

“With your face. Unasked.”

“You had food that was about to expire.”

“In a month.”

“Like you would’ve eaten it within the month,” Kara scoffed, still draped over Lena like a blanket. “You and Maggie eat more takeout than me.”

“That’s physically impossible.” Alex crossed her arms, leaning against the wall by the door. “You eat the contents of one Chinese food place a day, minimum.”

“I cook!”

Alex raised an eyebrow.

“…Lena cooks.”

“But not today! My waffle iron is out of commission.”

“Oh, no! What happened?”

I tried to synthesize 260 with cast iron.

“Experiment gone wrong.”

Kara laughed, squeezing tighter. “I really, really missed you.”

“Hate to break up the hug fest,” said Maggie, approaching the open door, “but I come bearing - um, green things?”

“Good save, babe,” Alex teased, dragging her in by the hand and very sneakily hiding what had to be a good gallon of mint chip ice cream, among other Danvers kitchen staples. “So! I have a big, tough cop girlfriend to protect me, you have waffles to eat - go, scoot, skedaddle!”

“Skedaddle?”

“Yes. Skedaddle.”

“Oh.” Kara removed her face from Lena’s shoulder and frowned, scrutinizing. “You’re sure?”

“Yes.”

“Because I know Eliza gave you a waffle iron back when she had hopes and dreams.”

“Get out of here.”

Lena grinned and, arms firmly around Kara’s waist, picked her up off the floor. “So long, farewell, auf wiedersehen, goodbye.”

“I love The Sound of Music,” Kara said, a little stunned. “Have you been working out?”

“I think my body’s just used to metabolizing solar energy now. I’m much more efficient.”

Lena set Kara down at the top of the stairs and took in her pink cheeks, her fluttering heart.

“Nice.”

“Mm-hm. Now, c’mon, before our favorite waiter’s shift ends.”

☆

The diner they went to for brunch was a long forgotten relic about as old as Lena. The menus were laminated, tastefully sparing in their use of clipart, and used one of the less ugly dyslexia-friendly fonts. There was, for whatever reason, a motif of farmland alien abductions in the decoration that they both found hilarious, and the waffles were always perfect, even when the chef stretched herself and went liège.

Unfortunately, the rush could not be beat, so they didn’t get to sit beneath the oil painting of a Grey pantsing George W. Bush, but they still scored a booth - the particularly cracked one by the sticker-plastered bathroom door.

Their serveur préféré was still on the clock, which was nice. His name was Pete, and he was funny without being overbearing, and very explicit about allergy information because his own daughter had a peanut problem.

“Hey! It’s been a while since I’ve seen your smiling faces.” Pete grinned, tapping his pen on his order pad with a drummer’s finesse. “What can I getcha?”

“Any specials today?”

“We have a caprese omelet, an Oreo short stack with hot chocolate syrup, a crème brûlée waffle with a little bit of kirsh and some house-candied black cherries, and a cinnamon roll waffle with vanilla bean cream cheese frosting.”

“I’ll take the kirsh, you take the cinnamon, we split them Power Rangers style?”

“Fight to the finish.” 

Kara pecked Lena on the lips and confirmed their order, along with coffee for Lena and a milkshake for herself.

“I’ll get that to you right away.”

With that, Pete vanished, leaving them alone in their beloved creaky booth. The table was small enough that their feet occupied the same longitudinal parallel, ankles knocking together. Kara retracted at the knee like she was at a Catholic school dance, hooking her heels over the rung between the chair’s legs and knocking her kneecaps into the bottom of the table itself. The only reason it didn’t go flying, or at least dislodge everything on it, was because Lena surged forwards and held it down.

Hands on Kara’s corners of the table, Lena grinned awkwardly and said, “Efficiency,” with a tiny shrug.

Kara laughed. 

“You can sprawl out. You’ve got long legs.”

“It’s okay.”

“I’m on the actual booth side, Kara, I have space to put my feet up.” Lena demonstrated, adjusting her sundress to conceal her feet when she tucked them up onto the cracked vinyl upholstery. 

Fussing with her glasses, Kara stretched her legs out, worrying her bottom lip between her teeth. “I just wanted to say I was sorry. About the phone call.”

“No, I get it. Alex pulled the same thing on Maggie when we went, um, exploring? A couple of months ago.” Lena toyed with the rim of her glass and mouthed Maaldoria. and Kara’s eyes widened in understanding. “You two don’t do well with the thought of losing each other. I get that.”

“I just - I felt like it was my fault. If I hadn’t gone flying off - chasing off! I meant chasing! - after…”

Lena gave a thin smile. “Me.”

“You didn’t know someone was going to kidnap her.” Kara sighed. “It’s just, I got into it with Maggie, and Alex really wants us to get along, so she tried to play peacemaker, and if I had just - behaved myself, none of this would’ve happened.”

“You and Maggie get along great!”

“Yeah, but when it comes to work, we disagree. More, lately.”

Lena reached over and took Kara’s fidgety hand in hers, running her thumb across the ridges of her knuckles. “Today, it looked like you two were fixing that.”

“I think we have.”

“It also looked like Maggie and Alex definitely needed a sock to hang on the door.”

“Ugh!” Kara squeezed her eyes shut and shook her head. “But, anyways, back to the point: I’m still sorry. I promised to be there for you, and you’re dealing with a lot right now, and I wasn’t. I shut you out, and that’s not - that’s not okay.”

“It was… office stuff. I’m not cleared to go back yet.”

“It wasn’t like that. We were there for Alex, not for any, um, work. Everything was just moving so fast, and I was so panicked - if Maggie hadn’t been there when I got the call, I don’t even know that I would’ve thought to bring her in.” Kara squeezed Lena’s hand in her own and looked her dead in the face. “I promise. They’re not fridging you.”

Lena nodded slowly. “Okay. I believe you. And I…”

Withhold, said Rhea’s voice in her ear, but Lena didn’t want to take that advice. Rhea was brilliant, but she didn’t have much by way of family or friends since her planet was gone. Shutting herself off from everyone probably made sense; if no one got close to her, she didn’t have to lose anyone else. Lena used to live like that, and it sucked. She didn’t want to live like that ever again.

“I was a little hurt. And I’ll probably be a little hurt for a while, but it’s just…” She sighed, waved her free hand flippantly. “Poking at an old wound. It’ll heal, and I’ll be fine, but for now, you just have to let it be.”

Kara nodded soberly. “Okay.” She pulled Lena’s hand close and kissed her knuckles. “I will let it be.”

“Thank you.” Lena’s cheeks heated, and she smiled at Kara across the table before leaning over and kissing her softly. “Apology accepted.”

Kara grinned against her lips, holding her hand tighter and kissing her back. Lena’s heart fluttered in her chest, and she wrapped her hand around the back of Kara’s neck, absently playing with her hair just to hear her breath hitch. 

They only really pulled apart because Pete, the angel, was walking up with their drinks. He set Kara’s chocolate shake, complete with its wobbly mountain of whipped cream, and Lena’s sedate-by-comparison black coffee down with a wink. “Waffles will be out in five minutes.”

“Thank you,” Lena said, clearing her throat. 

Once Pete was gone, the two of them broke out in a fit of giggles that neither of them could quite manage to control. Just when they thought they had it handled, Kara dropped her head and let out a sigh. When she straightened up, there was a smudge of whipped cream on her eyebrow, and Lena managed to stifle her laughter only long enough to arch an eyebrow of her own, cluing Kara in. 

Finally, they petered out, and Kara looked at Lena for a long moment. “I love it when you’re happy.”

Lena bit her lip. “You’re such a sap.”

“Only for you.”

“Liar. You’re a sap for everything.” Lena reached over and cupped Kara’s cheek, thumbing off a residual streak of white from her temple. She drew the pad of her thumb into her mouth and licked it clean. “It’s one of the many reasons you’re so wonderful.”

A megawatt beam glowed on Kara’s face, and Lena nearly spilled coffee in her lap, she was so distracted by the sight of it. Thankfully, she managed not to wreck her dress, and her drink actually made it into her mouth. 

“So, how’s business?”

Lena grinned, ear to ear, and took another sip. “Good. And top secret.” 

“Off the record - not even a hint?”

“Things are… still in synthesis.”

Kara squinted. “Was that a hint? Was that a pun?”

Coyly, Lena shrugged. “Was it?”

Kara stretched out one penny loafered foot and nudged Lena’s knee. “Don’t distract me by being cute.”

“Right now, everything’s just getting started. I’m gathering supplies, delegating work so I can actually get hands-on with this project.”

“Ooh!”

“And once everything is finished and tested and perfect, you will be the first one I tell.”

Kara nodded, and Pete swooped in, plates balanced on his fingertips. “Crème brûlée and cinnamon roll waffles - and some hot syrup for the table.”

“You’re a miracle worker, Pete.”

“All in a day’s work. Enjoy!”

Lena looked down at her little baby lièges with their crackly sugar and all the little pockets of custardy goodness, then over at Kara’s waffles, which appeared to be actual cinnamon rolls cooked in a waffle iron instead of in an oven. Quick as a flash - or, perhaps, the Flash - she scooped up her fork and stole a bite off Kara’s plate before her girlfriend even had the chance to blink.

“Hey!”

“This was your idea,” Lena said, popping the bite into her mouth. “Mm. Incredible.”

Kara’s jaw, dropped out of pure shock, clacked shut, and she grinned, eyes calculating. She tilted her head so her glasses slid down her nose and stared at Lena’s waffles for a split second before carving out a bite that Lena was certain had at least two nuggets of pearl sugar.

Judging by the crunch, she was right. 

“So good,” Kara groaned. 

Lena dragged the tines of her fork through the burnt sugar, listening to the crackle, then stuck her fork in her mouth. “Mm-hm. This is the only place worth ordering specials from.”

“Agreed.” Kara reached out and tried to nab a cherry, and while she managed to grab one, Lena caught her wrist before she could abscond with it. 

She was actually in a good mood. Working with Rhea gave her a sense of purpose that she sorely needed - the same sense of purpose that drove her as Galaxy Girl, the same sense of purpose that had her dedicate five years of her life to BioMax, the same sense of purpose that felt lacking since she’d been benched and Jack had died.

And because she was in a good mood, she felt like being a little shit.

Looking Kara square in the eyes, she ate the cherry out of her fingers. The sugary syrup clinging to its skin was sticky on her fingertips, and Lena may or may not have licked it off them.

Kara, wide-eyed, was frozen in her chair. 

Lena grinned, kissed her fingertips before letting go of her wrist. “Delicious.”

“You,” Kara breathed, “are the worst.”

“Yup. Sit with me.”

Kara picked up her plate and slid around to the bench side of the table, scooting in close enough that she and Lena were sat hip-to-hip, thigh-to-thigh. Lena stabbed a forkfull of cherries and offered it to her, knocking their knees together. Kara put a hand on Lena’s thigh - barely above her knee - and took the bite. 

Lena realized, only too late, that Kara Zor-El Danvers could play dirtier than the best of them. She chewed, made some soft, indecent noise, and swallowed like she hadn’t just shorted out the supercomputer in Lena’s head with magnetism.

The competition leaked out of their meal, and they ended up half in each other’s laps, feeding each other waffles and reigning themselves back from delving too deep into the realm of PDA. Lena went through only two cups of coffee, but two pitchers of ice water, by the time their plates were clean.

“Pick a number,” she said.

“Hm… Four.”

This was, probably, Lena’s favorite part about eating restaurant foods. She liked tipping well, and she could afford to do it; her usual date had worked as a waitress and appreciated just how necessary those tips were, but since Supergirl didn’t have a Social Security number and Kara Danvers was a cub reporter, she couldn’t always go balls to the wall on gratuity, which was where this game came in.

Kara picked a number - any number was allowed, but she usually stayed between two and five - and that was how many times the price of their meal the server got tipped.

“Four it is.”

As if on cue, Pete appeared. “Are you two ready for the check?”

“Yes, but can we get an order of fries to go?”

“Of course. I’ll be right back with that.”

True to his word, Pete returned inside of five minutes with a recycled paper clamshell full of steaming hot fries and the check. Lena scribbled down a triple digit tip, tucked her debit card into the check folder, and took a bite of a fry. 

Crispy, golden, and just a little spicy - just how they liked it. 

Once the payment had been processed, they ducked out, wandering vaguely towards the park and munching, arm in arm. 

“So, what’s - oh, my god.” 

Someone had stopped off inside a tiny bookstore with a No Pets policy and left their sesame shiba inu outside. 

“Hello, gorgeous,” Lena murmured, closing their takeout box and reaching out to let the puppy sniff her hand. 

The puppy sniffed her, then the knee of Kara’s jeans, and barked softly, demanding pets.

Kara dropped to the pavement, allowing the dog to crawl into her lap, and started scratching behind her ears. “What a good girl! Huh? What a good girl!”

Lena crouched down beside her and ran her hand down the puppy’s back, revealing a blue collar with a name tag. “Button, huh?”

Button stuck out her tongue and rolled onto her side.

“Oh, my god. You want a belly rub, huh?” Lena dragged her knuckles along the edge of Button’s stomach, testing the waters. Button rolled onto her back, and Lena moved on to properly petting her belly. “That’s a great belly. Ten out of ten, would pet again.”

Button licked her wrist, tail wagging. 

“Now I know why they named you that,” Kara cooed, scritching under Button’s chin. “Because you are so freaking cute!”

Squeaking back a pretty spot on tonal mimicry, Button play-nipped at Kara’s hand, and she let out a surprised giggle before, dramatically, flopping back onto the sidewalk.

“I am defeated!” she howled. “I am no match for the great and powerful Button!”

Button yipped, padding up Kara’s stomach and licking her chin. Kara peeled one eye open and gasped.

“You have healed me with your magical kisses! How can I ever repay you?”

Boof!

Button rolled onto her back, belly up for more petting, and no one was in any position to deny her. Kara and Lena sat there on the sidewalk for a good ten minutes, just petting puppy tummies and murmuring increasingly nonsensical things to Button, who ate it up with a spoon.

After those ten minutes were up, a harried-looking guy in his late twenties came out with a recycled tote full of books and laughed. “Oh, my god, are you guys okay?”

“Yep. She seemed bored, so we stopped to play with her. Was that okay?”

“Totally fine. She’s kind of high energy, isn’t that right, Button? Huh?”

Button scrambled out of Lena’s arms and pawed at the guy’s jeans. 

“Did you have fun?”

Boof!

“Yeah? Good girl!”

Kara and Lena stood, brushing themselves off. “She’s a real sweetie pie.”

“Yeah.” The guy shouldered his bag and untied Button’s leash with one hand, sticking out the other to shake. “I’m Kyle.”

“Nice to meet you. I’m Kara, and this is my girlfriend, Lena.”

To his credit, Kyle didn’t so much as look twice at Lena, or give any indication that he made the connection between face and name. Instead, he just asked, “You two have a dog?”

“No. We’re both really busy. It wouldn’t be fair to get a dog and leave them alone all the time.”

“Well, if we see you around, I’m sure Button would love to catch up.”

Button wagged her tail and licked Lena’s shin in confirmation before going still, listening. Then she barked and raced off in the other direction, and Kyle was dragged off after her. 

“I think she heard a friend,” Kara said, grinning. 

“Yeah?” Lena listened for a moment; sure enough, about half a block away, Button was sniffing animatedly with another puppy, and Kyle was chatting away with someone. “She really does have boundless energy.”

“I love dogs.”

“I’ve noticed.”

“Like you don’t!” Kara grinned, draping an arm around Lena’s shoulders and kissing her temple, fry box in hand. “Do you think Alex and Maggie will let us dog sit?”

“They’re getting a dog?”

“And naming her Gertrude.”

“That is a horrible dog name.”

“Yeah, but they’re happy about it.” 

Lena knocked her head into Kara’s cheek. “They’ll definitely let us dog sit. They have to go on vacation eventually, right?”

Laughing, Kara laid her head on top of Lena’s. “It’s going to end up being some weird work trip with two minutes of sightseeing. I bet.”

“What, like they run off to hunt down some Plutonian drug smuggler and take a selfie in front of the Boston Bean?”

“Probably.” Kara gasped, stopping dead in the middle of the sidewalk. “Wanna go see our puppies?”

Lena’s brow furrowed. “We don’t have puppies.”

“No, no, no, the ones we delivered.”

“That was, what, two, three months ago?”

“Yeah. They’re old enough to go home with families now, or to be taken on walks by volunteers.”

“You just want a puppy.”

“I really, really do.”

“Let’s go walk some puppies, then.”

☆

They each ended up with one puppy to walk - Kara picked one called Junior, who looked exactly like her mother, and Lena ended up selecting the runt of the litter, ironically dubbed Gigantor - after spending about half an hour just playing with what was left of the litter. Three of the four puppies, as well as their mother, remained, because nobody wanted a pit.

“Bad reputation,” Shelby said with a sigh. “And they don’t deserve it, either. They’re just dumb little noodles - they just want to be loved, and they’re real devoted, too.”

“I bet.”

“Who adopted the one puppy?”

“Oh. This cute little girl came in with her parents after seeing Supergirl and Galaxy Girl on our website with these puppies. Total hero worship - really cute.”

“Huh,” Kara said, nudging Lena in the ribs with her elbow. “You don’t say.”

Lena just wrapped her arm around Kara’s waist and swallowed a grin. 

Once they’d been given the rundown of Junior and Gigantor’s walking requirements - Junior was scared of traffic and Gigantor had pretty low stamina, both for walking and for socializing, due to her size - they collected some plastic baggies and two leashes and started for the park.

They went at a lazy pace to give Gigantor a shot at keeping up. She stayed close to her big sister, following her stoically down the street and stopping when she stopped. When they were about two blocks from the entrance to the park, a silver sedan piloted by a dead-eyed man in a golf shirt swerved through the intersection against the lights. 

Kara, diligent about traffic law, dragged her jaywalk-prone girlfriend back. Junior cowered away from the car, and Gigantor started barking. At ten weeks, she was the size her siblings had been at one month, and her sandy coat harkened back to teddy bears. She looked like the least threatening or intimidating thing on the planet after a ladybug or a baby bunny.

Which is why the sound that came out of her was so shocking. She let out a ferocious snarl, barking after Polo Shirt’s taillights, standing firm between him and her big sister.

Once the car had turned another corner and disappeared, she turned around and licked Junior’s face. That behavioral about-face was so startling that, for a moment, neither Lena nor Kara moved or made a sound. Only once people started moving around them, casting a wide berth, did they snap back into action, scooping up their respective puppies and bustling across the intersection.

Safely on the other side of the street, Lena ducked her head and planted a kiss on one of Gigantor’s ears. “Good girl.”

Gigantor licked her shoulder and snuffled. 

The park started out with a gentle hill, asphalt flanked on either side by municipal grass, and Junior went nuts over it, scrambling out of Kara’s arms and rolling around in the dirt. Gigantor was hot on her heels, and that twenty foot hill took twenty minutes to summit. 

The early afternoon sun cast a halo around Kara’s head, and Lena just sort of stared for a moment.

“Ooh! Street fair!” Kara pointed downhill, then turned to gage Lena’s reaction. “What?”

“You’re just… stupendously pretty.”

Kara went pink, and Lena reached over and took her hand. “C’mon. You said there was a street fair?”

“First of the season, probably. Wanna take a look?”

“Sure. Why not?”

Downhill they went, hand-in-hand.

The long center path was flanked by pop-up booths and tents full of hand-knit sweaters and homemade soaps and crystal pendants. About half a mile off, Lena could see a bounce house and a King Kong half-moon ride, and the smell of cotton candy was thick in the air. 

“I love these,” Kara sighed, hands swinging. “Everyone’s so happy, and there’s so much fun stuff to do.”

“Did you ever go to them when you were a kid?” 

“They didn’t have bouncy castles where I was born - not like that, anyway.”

“I meant in Midvale.”

“Oh. Oh, yeah, all the time! Tiny little beach town? There were street fairs, like, every weekend. I had so many bottles of sand art. So. Many.”

Lena laughed, picturing a tiny teenaged Kara surrounded by jars upon endless jars of stripy rainbow sand, grinning ear to ear besides an exasperated Alex. 

“How about you? Are street fairs a thing in Metropolis?”

“Only in summer. They had tree markets for Christmas, though. Fir trees and wreathes and maple syrup from Vermont. I loved it. We would get these big five gallon jugs of syrup that would last us all year, and my mom always got a tiny tree so I could put the star on top.” Lena smiled softly, remembering the red glitter their ornaments shed all over everything. They had scarlet sparkles everywhere until July at least; two months after she moved in with the Luthors, she shook the last of the previous Christmas’ glitter out of her shoes and nearly suffocated under a fresh wave of loneliness. “I was a very… exuberant child.”

“The Danvers’ don’t celebrate Christmas, but Eliza makes these amazing sufganiyot with raspberry jam. Definitely worth the tree trade.”

“I bet. Eliza is incredible.”

“I’ll tell her you said that.”

Lena’s ears burned. “Must you?”

“Like you didn’t already gush about her, to her face, all Thanksgiving long.” Kara squeezed Lena’s hand and grinned slyly. 

“Mortifying.”

“No! Eliza liked you.”

Lena balked, unsure of how to respond. Out of the corner of her eye, she caught a familiar word and darted towards the stand. 

“Vegetable espresso?” Kara had bolted after her, wrinkling her nose at the sign. “Why?”

“Well, the flavor of the mushrooms helps balance out the bitterness of the coffee.” The guy behind the stand offered Lena a waxed paper shot glass. “Free sample?”

Lena smiled and downed the coffee like a shot. “Oh. Wow.”

Usually, she hated cold espresso - it always tasted like the pot it was brewed in - but somehow, the portobello helped. It just tasted like coffee. “That’s fascinating.”

“Fix-it fascinating or delicious fascinating?” Kara asked, staring Lena down over the rims of her glasses.

“Delicious fascinating.”

The guy behind the stand beamed, standing a little taller. “We sell it by the bag, if you’re interested.”

“Sounds good.”

As the kid scooped a bag of beans and dehydrated mushrooms, Kara settled her weight onto one hip, pensive. “It’s actually good?”

“I mean, I actually like vegetables and black coffee, but yeah.”

“Hm.”

Lena laughed. “Do you want to try it?”

“Sure,” Kara said, leaning in and kissing her. It was gentle and brief and Lena dropped her wallet for it; Kara just sighed when she pulled back. 

“So?”

“Wouldn’t mind it in the morning.” 

Lena stuck her tongue out at Kara, who just beamed at her and knelt to pick up her wallet, which she folded back into Lena’s hand with sure fingers. Lena’s fingers were much less sure - or, perhaps, just distracted - as she payed for her bag of beans and grabbed a business card, shoving both into her pocket. 

They steadied, though, when they tangled into Kara’s. Hands swinging and puppies in tow, they meandered down the path, skirting screaming kids and impulse buy-beleaguered pedestrians and picking up more than their fair share of fair food. Or the central California equivalent thereof.

“There should be cotton candy.”

“What, pretzels aren’t good enough for you?”

“Nothing can beat a wad of fluffy sugar the size of a small child, I’m sorry.”

“It always surprises me to see evidence of your sweet tooth,” Kara said, gesturing with her Brobdingnagian pretzel. 

“You’ve seen me eat twenty four chocolate frosted doughnuts in one sitting.”

“Yeah, but that was an emergency.”

Lena shrugged. “I like sugar, I just don’t always seek it out. Being able to eat unlimited everything is kind of a recent development.”

“Well, I’m glad that development was made. Pretzel?”

“Why not?” 

Kara offered it Lena’s way, and she took a bite. 

“Good, right?”

“Yeah…” Lena grinned, puckish, “but it’s not cotton candy.”

“Well, if you don’t want it, I’m more than happy to eat a wad of dough the size of my ribcage.” Kara knocked her hip into Lena’s and held the pretzel between her teeth, shifting her grip on the leash so Junior wasn’t directly in the path of someone carrying a tie-dyed body pillow taller than they were. “Ooh, strongman!”

Eyes wide as she glanced between the red metal game, topped with a bell that read ‘It Takes a REAL Man To Ring The Bell’ and her girlfriend with actual super strength, Lena hissed, “Kara, we can’t.”

“What? We can moderate. You’re great at controlling yourself. You never even accidentally broke someone’s bones.”

“No, just lots of furniture.”

“Well, play or not, I believe in you.” Kara grinned. “And I’m gonna play.”

Lena rolled her eyes fondly and took Junior, murmuring, “This is gonna be fun, huh, baby?”

Junior barked and sat down, wagging her tail in what Lena could only assume was anticipation.

Kara handed over a five and picked up the sledgehammer. Making eye contact with Lena, she made a big show of the hammer being impossibly heavy, setting it down in the dirt on the side of the road with a little puff of dust, cheeks round around a mouthful of pretzel. She wiped her hands on the seat of her jeans, rubbed her palms together, and shot Lena a wink over her shoulder before picking it up again. 

“You got this, sunshine,” Lena drawled, fighting a goofy smile.

“Fanks.”

Kara picked up the hammer and swung in a smooth arc. She hit the lever square, and Lena could see just how much she was holding back in the way she held herself, the way she choked up on the sledgehammer. 

She scored ninety out of one hundred, just shy of the bell, and gave an apple pie shrug. “Pretty good, huh?”

“You’d score higher if you worked out,” Lena teased, kissing her cheek. 

“She’d’a scored higher,” the gamerunner said, “if she were a real man.”

Kara bit back a snicker, but Lena had sat through too many business meetings with too many old men to laugh it off. “Darling, hold the dogs.”

“Of - of course.”

Kara took the leashes, and Lena’s bag, bouncing on her toes as she walked up to the game in her sundress and her ballet flats and flawlessly applied makeup. “Five bucks to play, right?”

“Sure.”

Lena pulled her wallet out of her dress pocket, fishing out a five and slapping it into the man’s hand, squinting with her head tilted back so she could stare down the length of her nose at him. 

“You got this, Lulu!”

She picked up the hammer, careful not to crack the wood, and swung.

With an earsplitting clang, she hit the lever, catapulting the weight up the back of the game and clean into the bell.

Which cracked.

Lena shrugged coolly and said, “Girl power,” before grabbing her bag and Gigantor’s leash and East Coast speed walking away, Kara’s arm around her.

“Okay. Number one, that was very impressive. Number two, that crack was tiny. Number three…” Kara swooped down and kissed Lena soundly, fingers curling into the curve of her waist and pulling her closer. “Girl power.”

Lena licked her lips. The mistake was one she definitely should have been able to avoid making. Hearing Lulu had shaken her, but maybe Kara was right, and nobody would notice.

“Nobody will notice,” Kara promised. “Do you know how many times I’ve ripped out of my clothes on the CatCo balcony and taken flight, and no one’s even noticed?”

“I’m going to need a moment to process the image of you ripping out of your clothes.”

“Take two, they’re small.”

Lena snorted, shaking her head. After a moment, once she’d collected herself, she asked, “Really? No one’s ever noticed?”

“When you work for Cat Grant, you don’t look up from your desk unless it’s your lunch break, and even then, it’s eyes on the elevator doors until you’re through them.”

“Incredible.”

“As in wow, or as in I don’t believe you, all of CatCo knows, including your boss, who once actually questioned you about it and necessitated the use of a shapeshifter to allay suspicion?”

“I… Thank god I haven’t met Cat Grant.”

“Oh, no! I think you two would get along really well.”

“Until I broke her office door. Which is now James’ office door. And he wouldn’t appreciate that very much, either.”

“You always fix your mistakes. It’d turn out okay.”

“Yeah, sure.”

“You do.” Kara stopped, voice earnest. “You’re good that way.”

Lena pressed her mouth tightly shut and leaned into Kara’s side, for just a moment.

“C’mon. I think I see cotton candy.”

☆

“I,” Lena said grandly, “am a genius.”

“Yes,” replied Kara, tucking two protectively-wrapped Mason jar terrariums into her gigantic reusable bag, “you are.”

Said bag contained too many souvenirs, which was precisely the point of street fairs. Lena’s weird yet delicious mushroom coffee, ten tiny terrariums, beeswax candles with dried plants embedded in the wax, local honey imbued with lavender and hibiscus and orange, bags of handmade candies in flavors ranging from apple cider caramel to za’atar taffy, and little hand-bound notebooks with homemade paper.

“Are you Hermione Granger?” 

“I wish.”

“That bag is absolutely Undetectably Expanded.”

“Now that you’ve guessed, I’m certain it’s not Undetectable.”

Kara snorted and ripped an organic doggy treat in two, offering the larger piece to Gigantor, who mostly just licked Kara’s fingers as she wolfed it down, tail wagging. Junior ate her piece with just as much puppy gusto, pawing at Kara’s shin through her jeans. 

“Aw, June bug, who’s a good girl?”

Junior barked, jumping up into the crook of Kara’s arm.

“That’s right! It’s you!”

Lena scratched behind Gigantor’s ears, smiling crookedly. “Don’t forget, she’s not our puppy.”

“I know.” Kara sighed, kissing the top of Junior’s head. “But she’s still cute, and she still deserves affection.”

“Yeah.” Lena adjusted the bag on her shoulder and her grip on Gigantor, freeing up a hand to take Kara’s. “Yeah, I guess so.”

On they wandered, past booths and games and rides. Part of Lena wanted to ride the half-moon, but more of her knew that, upon giving it a shot, she would absolutely rip through the metal, and there was no excusing that, no explaining it away, no ‘whoopsie, how’d that happen.’

Until she reacclimatized, until her powers leveled out again, she was going to have to be a lot more careful. 

That thought, and Kara’s warm hand in hers, kept Lena pretty preoccupied, but Kara had no such distractions in her head, and she burst out laughing at something she saw.

“I zhor,” she whispered, giggling, “look.”

Lena looked. 

Lena cackled.

“Superhero stuffies?”

“I have to tell Winn and James that there’s a Guardian plushie floating around out there.” 

The booth they were laughing over had more than just a little fuzzy Guardian with a little fuzzy shield. It had every National City super in plush form, plus toy replicas of their weapons and tools, costume pieces - everything a fan could ask for. They even had stuff for the one-offs, like a Flash swim cap and Silver Banshee masks. 

While Kara finagled a shot of Barry’s memorabilia, Lena took a picture of a Livewire patch that read Shock Jock, and a few other things, just so she could covertly get the patch in front of her eerie black eyes. 

“I can’t believe they have the batons,” Lena murmured, staring at them where they hung in the back of the frame. “I can’t believe - she’s up there.”

“National City loves Galaxy Girl,” said Kara softly, lowering her phone. “She’s never done anything but good.”

“She’s got good focus.”

“Mm-hm.” Kara set Junior down and walked in closer to the booth, looping the leash through her belt. Two minutes later, she came back with a pair of foam batons and something with Galaxy Girl’s armor plating silkscreened on. “Cover me.”

“What?”

“I’m changing my shirt, and I don’t want to hide out in a PortaPotty.”

Lena rolled her eyes and pushed Kara off the road and onto the grass, behind a tree, where she stood with her feet planted and her arms wide, dogs playing close by. “You’re ridiculous.”

“You love it. Turn around.”

In the time it took for Lena to turn, Kara had dropped into a comic cover-worthy three point pose. Her hoodie was too baggy to really look like Lena’s armor, but the shimmery purple plating, the low-hanging hood, and the batons made a pretty picture. She rose effortlessly to her feet, twirling the batons, mimicking Lena’s fighting style with above-par accuracy.

Lena swallowed hard, pushing Kara’s hood down and tucking stray blonde curls behind her ears, cupping the back of her neck. She stretched up and kissed Kara, backing her up against the trunk. 

“So,” Kara said, eyes glassy and a little breathless, “I’m thinking I found my Hallowe’en costume.”

“I’m thinking…” Lena sighed deep and kissed Kara again, right on her forehead. “C’mon. Back to the booth.”

“Why?”

“Galaxy Girl’s not the only hero in National City.”

They filled Lena’s bag with some of everything, Kara holding the bag open as Lena packed like she was playing Tetris. Last minute, Lena saw something and, on impulse, said, “That, too, in a six, if you have it.”

“Everyone loves Supergirl,” said the girl behind the booth with a knowing nod. “Cape chasers in this city have good taste.”

Lena blushed, but she kept her chin square. “I’m her number one fan.”

“So’s everyone else.”
With a shrug and a grin, Lena paid and took her last purchase. “Have a good day.”

“What was that about?” Kara asked, equally pink-cheeked. “‘Number one fan,’ really?”

“It’s true,” said Lena with a shrug, tucking it into her bag. She linked her arm with Kara’s and kissed her on the cheek. “Wouldn’t be dating her if I wasn’t.”

Kara shrugged Lena’s bag higher on her shoulder and grinned from ear to ear. “So, what did you buy, O Number One Fan?”

“Something I’m not changing into behind a tree.”

Very nearly tripping over her own feet, Kara gave Lena a wide-eyed stare that flitted back and forth between her and the bag. “What?”

Lena hummed, innocent as a choir girl, and fluttered her eyelashes. 

“I’m…” Kara groaned, knocking her forehead into Lena’s shoulder. “Never going to get that image out of my head.”

“Good image, though?”

“No kidding.”

Junior, at Kara’s feet, plopped down on the blacktop and whined.

“Tired puppy?”

“Let’s take them home,” Lena offered, “and then come back?”

“Sounds good.”

Lena had been carrying Gigantor for most of the afternoon, just to avoid tiring her out, but Junior had finally caught up to her sister, which meant their walk was just about over. Kara carried Junior back to the shelter, and they signed the puppies back in with a drawn-out goodbye.

“Come back any time,” Shelby said, smiling brightly as she clicked the pen shut. “No one ever walks Junior enough to get her this calm.”

“We’ll be back, right?”

“Absolutely.”

With that promise made, Kara and Lena made their way back towards the park, pace much quicker, and soon, they were passing the superhero swag booth again, and Kara’s face went cherry red.

“Supergirl underwear. Really?”

“Oh, I wish.”

Kara let out a strangled noise.

“No. It’s a Supergirl bikini.”

“Next weekend, we’re going to the beach.”

Lena grinned, nodding jauntily. “Sounds good to me.”

Up ahead, they spotted the end of the twin rows of booths, marked off by a significantly steeper hill than the one that opened the fair. 

“I guess we did cover a lot of ground before.”

“Yes, but not all of it.” Lena tapped Kara’s nose with another cloud of cotton candy. “And this path loops back around, which means we’ll be right on track to head back towards your apartment.”

“We should drop off Alex and Maggie’s terrariums.”

“I can’t believe they make bonsai in a jar.”

“It’s so cute.” Kara fished one out of Lena’s bag and inspected it. “So cute.”

“And so tiny.”

“It’s proportionate!”

“I’m telling Maggie you made a short joke.”

“You wouldn’t.”

“We tiny girlfriends have to stick together!”

“You’re five foot six!”

“You’re five foot nine. Comparatively, I am short.”

Kara rolled her eyes. “If you say so.”

“I do.”

As they approached the last booths, Lena started running, dragging Kara behind her, and she stopped just as suddenly.

“How much?”

“Oh. Sand art’s free.”

Lena looked up at Kara, hesitating just a hair. “Wanna?”

“Why not?” said Kara, way too excited for such nonchalant words, and got to work.

The booth was really four folding tables set up in a square, covered in glass bottles and buckets of colored sand with two funnels and two scoops per color. A few kids were finishing their bottles on the other side of the booth, commemorative free refill cups forgotten, and Lena nudged about thirty ounces of grape soda away from the blue sand with a smile playing over her lips. 

She watched Kara for a moment, the intense focus on her face, the light in her eyes. “So, what got you to do these the first time? Back in Midvale.”

“Jeremiah. He thought it would be a good way to help me control my strength. The glass is fragile, so no one really notices if it breaks, and it’s sort of meditative.”

“Did it help?”

“Yeah. And it was fun.” Kara tilted a tiny bottle in the light, lips pursed. “And it reminded me of home.”

“The Crystal Mountains.”

“If the weather was right, you could see clear through them to the horizon. To the sun.”

“It must have been beautiful.”

“It was.” Satisfied with her choice - an empty perfume bottle from, easily, the 1890s with flowers etched into the inside walls - Kara started to fill the bottle with sand. She tilted it so the first color caught inside the grooves, marking out the blooms in violet before pouring in a gradient of reds and pinks. 

About two minutes into this endeavor, Lena decided she’d join in, too, picking a scrubbed-clean minibar bottle just for the challenge. Because of the size, she couldn’t manage any fancy patterns, but she managed fairly even black, red, and grey stripes all the way up. Focusing on regulating the pattern, Lena managed not to break the bottle, even if it did take her ten minutes to fill a one fluid ounce container. 

Kara, munching on what was basically a bag of artisanal Pop Rocks, waited patiently for Lena to finish and, because she couldn’t not, leave a tip in the quart container on the front table. Once Lena was done, bottle screwed shut and tucked into her pocket, Kara ducked her head and opened her mouth so the candy popped in her ear.

Lena jumped, then started to laugh. “Rao!”

“Did I scare you?”

“You startled me.” Lena grinned, shaking her head. “Pop Rocks were my favorite as a kid. Science candy.”

“These aren’t Pop Rocks. They’re ‘carbonated plum and maple sugar crystals.’”

“They’re Pop Rocks.”

Kara shook another mouthful onto her tongue and practically unhinged her jaw, popping noises filling the air. Lena linked her arm with Kara’s and swayed into her side, stealing a few and sprinkling them into her mouth. 

Plum and maple sugar and carbonation. Who knew?

The path beneath their feet began to turn, and they followed it in companionable silence broken only by the fizzing candy in their mouths. Only once they exited the park, and had gotten halfway back, did either of them say a word.

“We should ding dong ditch the terrariums,” Kara said. “Right? Since Maggie and Alex are having… ‘alone time,’ or whatever the kids are calling it these days.”

“The kids?” Lena wrinkled her nose, tucking the candy into her pocket. “You’re twenty seven.”

“A grown woman, exactly.”

“They’re both older than you.”

Kara shrugged, smiling. 

“Ding dong ditch, it is.”

They swung by Alex’s place, knocking rapidly on the window and leaving their two tiny trees on the outer sill before racing off along the skyline, more than a little giddy. Finally, scaling down the side of Kara’s building and entering her apartment through the window, Lena set down her bag.

“What did James say about the doll?”

“Let me check.” Kara toed off her shoes and flopped onto the couch. “James is glad people like the Guardian enough to make toys; Winn just keysmashed.”

“Really?”

“Oh, and he apparently needs twelve of them.”

Lena snickered, gently shutting the window before laying down on top of Kara. Her legs slotted between Kara’s, and her elbows braced on either side of her hips. “That sounds about right.”

“Good thing you went all out on memorabilia.”

“Hey.” Lena glared, all good humor. “We went all out on memorabilia.”

“Yeah, we did.” 

Kara wrapped her arms around Lena, one hand splayed over the top of her back, fingers stretching along the line of her neck. Lena snuggled down, laying her cheek on Kara’s collarbone, and smiled softly, closing her eyes. She never wanted to move from that spot, to pop the perfect soap bubble preserving that moment.

Which was, of course, why her phone rang.

“Grab that for me,” she grumbled. “Left pocket.”

“Gotcha.” Kara fished into Lena’s left pocket and retrieved her phone, passing it to her, and the candy, which she kept for herself.

“It’s probably Jess. I sent her pictures of the superhero booth; there was some stuff I know she would have liked.”

“What stuff?”

“Um…”

It wasn’t Jess. 

Rhea had an idea for 260 synthesis based off Lena’s notes.

“Is that work?”

“Yeah.”

“Go for it. Have fun.”

“You sure?”

Kara nodded, genuine. “You love your work.”

“I love spending time with you, too.”

“I know, silly.” Kara kissed Lena’s forehead, then pushed up onto her elbows, sitting Lena up via transitive power. “Now, go. Scoot. Skedaddle.”

Lena got to her feet, pausing for a moment to consider whether or not she should bring her bag or leave it on Kara’s floor. In the end, she decided to come back for it later, and straightened up, returning to Kara’s side to kiss her goodbye.

When she did, she couldn’t help but laugh. Kara’s mouth was fizzing.

I really, really, really, really love her, she thought, kissing her again. 

“Be safe,” she murmured. “No club soda, or you’ll explode.”

“Ooh, I’m so scared.” Kara ran her fingers through Lena’s hair, hand trailing down her neck to her shoulders, giving her a fond squeeze. “Now, quit procrastinating. Go be incredible.”

“I’ll do my best.”

Notes for the Chapter:

If you read through all eight thousand and eight words of that, congratulations! You have absorbed the last happy thing in this fic for basically all I have planned out until the end of the finale! Please cling to Kara being a beautiful bi mess over her girlfriend in a Supergirl bikini, Lena's dress having pockets, puppies, brunch, good tipping, and Fighting The Patriarchy for as long as you can, and feel free to tell me what part of the date was your favorite.

Or yell at me for taking so long.

Take your pick.
