20. Chapter 20

Summary for the Chapter:

Set during 2x20: City of Lost Children. Everything goes to shit.

Notes for the Chapter:

I messed with the science a little bit, just because what they went with in the show was super inconsistent. You probably won't notice, but I figured I should leave a disclaimer in case any of you did.

“Rhea’s waiting for you,” Hector said in lieu of greeting. “By your private lab.”

“Good.”

“No one goes into your private lab.”

“She and I are working on a top priority project together.” Lena eyed Hector, whose self-identified spidey senses appeared to be tingling. “Has she given you any reason to mistrust her?”

“Not particularly.”

“Well, she’s given me reason.”

Hector’s eyes widened, and his hands fluttered nervously. 

“And she’s given me more reason to trust her. Besides, this project is important enough that I can look past it.”

“Are you going to run it by the board?”

“Emailed them the proposal as soon as Rhea signed on. Probably won’t hear back until Monday, but the likelihood that we’ll get anything worth fuss done by then is slim.”

Hector frowned, but his hands moved back into a more neutral position. “I’ll be right here.”

“Much appreciated.” With what she hoped was a reassuring smile, Lena headed off to her lab.  Usually, she stopped off and changed clothes before she started working with molten metal, or even before she set foot inside her more hands-on workspace. Today, though, she hesitated. Rhea, with her regal bearing and tailored clothes, had never seen Lab Lena, and even though they were partners in this now, even though Lena was funding the project and, therefore, should be the one to impress, Lena couldn’t bring herself to dress down. Even her slightly casual weekend wear felt inappropriate. 

Closing her eyes, Lena focused her hearing and listened. Rhea didn’t sound impatient; her heart rate wasn’t elevated in frustration, and she wasn’t pacing or tapping her foot or drumming her fingers to fill the passive wait with something. Lena could probably spare thirty seconds to grab her spare office clothes.

But just because she could, didn’t mean she would. The fact that Rhea was waiting so patiently made Lena less willing to prolong the lull, so she steeled herself and strode in.

“Lena,” said Rhea warmly, rising from a lab bench with fluid ease. “I’m sorry to have interrupted your… weekend? I know there’s a custom of leisure days on this planet, but this project is very important to the both of us.”

“No need to apologize,” Lena assured her. “I wasn’t really doing much, just - I was with my girlfriend.”

“Things are better?”

“I think so. We talked a little. She didn’t mean to hurt me.”

“The ones we love are in the best position to hurt us, whether they intend to or not.” Rhea’s squared shoulders suddenly looked weighted with a world of pain, and Lena wanted to say something, to try and comfort her. She didn’t get the chance, though, because Rhea looked at her and smiled. “You look lovely, by the way.”

“Oh! Thank you. I don’t usually wear this sort of thing; my mother would give me hell for it.”

“Your mother?”

“Adoptive mother.” Lena flashed a quick beam, all surface, and rolled a hair elastic off her wrist. “You said you had an idea on synthesizing 260?”

“Yes. Your alloy was what inspired me, actually. I ran the numbers and, with nuclear fusion, it might be the perfect Terran source for 260.”

“I was considering that, too, but the addition of bismuth and titanium make it too weak a conductor for what we have in mind, and then the charge is all wrong. I even considered adding more iron - ”

“But it still didn’t quite work?”

Lena nodded, lips pressed into a thin line, pondering the death of her waffle iron.

“You’ve only been working on this for, what, a day? Isn’t there some bromide on this planet about expecting to accomplish great things in so short a period of time?”

“Rome, yes, but we don’t have one million, nine thousand, four hundred and ninety one days to do this. We both have planets to save.” With that, Lena twisted her hair tie around the base of her bun with a punctuative snap and put her hands on her hips in a posture she definitely got from her girlfriend. “Let’s get to work.”

And so they did. Using the large-scale generator ring L Corp was trying to pitch to city planners to power whole urban landscapes without a carbon footprint, they were able to achieve star-heart levels of pressure - the levels of pressure necessary to fuse atoms of one element into different, denser ones - without a particle accelerator. That, in and of itself, was a feat worth celebrating, and ordinarily, Lena would have called Kara right away to talk about it.

But these were not ordinary times, nor did the passage of time seem ordinary. Once they had synthesized enough 260 to fuel the reaction that would, effectively, rip a stable hole through the fabric of space, it was just a matter of sustaining that hole safely, which meant it was definitely Lena’s time to shine. 

Sixteen hours into the math, she got a call from Jess, acting as a liaison for the Board. 

“We’re in,” she said, in lieu of a more traditional greeting. 

“Everyone agreed?”

“Everyone agreed, but, actually Scriven and Waters both think there’s something more your partner needs to be doing.”

Lena’s brow furrowed. “And that might be what, exactly?”

“She’s an alien scientist with an obvious history in seats of power: they think she should fill a seat.”

Saying nothing, Lena crossed one arm over her chest, pressing the other tight to the sides of her ribs, squeezing herself. “Rhea’s not going to stay on Earth, Jess. This is her getting home. We can’t - we won’t ask her to give up everything she’s worked so hard for just to fill a seat.” 

“It’s a good look. L Corp, striding out amongst the stars, stomping out a legacy of xenophobia through a philanthropic partnership.”

“Don’t you think I know that?”

“I think you like working with her. I think you’ve ignored my last seven calls because you’ve been so focused on working with her.”

Lena opened her mouth to apologize, but Jess steamrollered on.

“I think that, if this machine works, she’s going to need at least a few weeks to regulate gravity and atmosphere conditions, and even longer to get supplies to fill the gap between terraforming restoration and agricultural equilibrium.” 

“Pía’s in on this, too.”

“We’re a much more communicative group, now that we’ve paired down. And we all think this is a good idea.”

“I can’t ask this of her.”

“Because you want her to say yes.” Jess sighed. “Lena…”

“Look. Now that the Board has approved, I have to go bring on some of our other engineers. It’ll speed up construction, and once - once we’ve got this thing operational, I will consider it.” Lena could hear the disapproval on Jess’ face, but she didn’t cave to it. “That’s the best I can give you, Jess, and you can tell the rest of the Board I said as much. I have to go.”

“Liz says hi.”

“Tell her I said hi back.”

“And she liked the merch.”

Lena smiled fleetingly. “I’m glad. Now, I have to go. I’ve got work to do.”

“Yeah, don’t we all.”

“Bye.”

“Bye.” Lena hung up and put her phone down, promptly going back to ignoring it. 

It took her longer than she would have liked to get back into a working headspace. The downside to working with Jess was that Jess was uniquely qualified to call out her bullshit, and thoroughly willing to do just that. Hector was an excellent assistant, but he wasn’t in a position to point out just why she was so reluctant to ask anything of Rhea. Jess, however, had been hired at one of the lowest points of Lena’s life. She’d been there for the trial, and Lillian, and everything that came after, so she knew.

Which would have been an excellent excuse for why Lena had ignored her phone calls, but that wasn’t the reason. In truth, she was just consumed by the work. Before Lex crossed over to the dark side, and before she met Jack, the plan for Lena had been Head of R&D at Luthor Corp, and she hadn’t minded. She’d been excited about it, actually, about working with her family, about building and innovating and using her brain. 

She’d never wanted to fill Lex’s shoes, but now that she had to, she had every intention of walking them in the right direction. 

Lena let out a sigh and squared her shoulders, redoing her topknot with far less precision and adjusting her glasses before sinking back into the math. Only half-focused on the world around her, she went to her lab door and called Hector’s name.

“Yes, Ms. Luthor?”

“Send a memo to R&D, please. Any engineers not currently working on a project are needed on this one.” 

“Of course. Are they coming into your lab, too?”

“Um.” Were they? “No. Construction is floor thirteen.”

“Got it. Also, you got a phone call - ”

“Already handled.”

And with that, Lena’s exponentially less-interested brain was 100% absorbed by the math. She hunkered down over her tablet, working away, and only snapped away from it when Rhea touched her shoulder. 

Actually snapped. She jerked like a gun had gone off, tablet clattering to her lab table.

“Sorry to startle you,” Rhea said, voice soothing.

“No, no, you’re fine.” Lena swallowed hard and checked her tablet - no damage, thank god. “What’s happening?”

“Moving to the construction phase.” Rhea offered her own tablet, of L Corp design, and showed Lena the memo. “How are the calculations coming?”

“They’re…” Lena sighed. “Theoretical. Right now! I’ve been toying with these principles in my free time, but now that I’m working on it all the time, I can’t help but worry that I’m missing something. I mean, your planet was clearly lightyears ahead of Earth scientifically - what if I can’t grasp the science behind this?”

“Lena.” Rhea smiled down at her, sitting next to her at the bench, hand still on her shoulder. “You are brilliant. Your mind is so far beyond any other on this planet, and more to the point, you are not from this planet. The limitations of Earthlings do not apply to you.”

“So far as education, information, supplies - ”

“Not anymore. You have me.”

Lena shook her head, saying nothing. 

“Now,” said Rhea, reaching up and tucking a stray lock of hair back behind Lena’s ear, “I’m really more of a chemical engineer than a mechanical one, but…”

“You’re a chemical engineer, and you came up with this?”

Rhea looked utterly delighted by the thought. “No. That’s kind of you to think, but no, Lena, I didn’t design this. It was - on my planet, this is akin to the public transportation systems you have here. We’ve had them for millennia. I did own the rights to the design, though, and that ownership would have gone down to my children.” There was an air of melancholy to her smile, then, but it wasn’t fading or falling away. “I’m glad to give it to you.”

“I - I just hope to do it justice.”

“You will. I know you will.”

Was it any wonder Lena’s work swallowed her whole?

☆

The construction in Lab Thirteen went faster than any other project of its magnitude in L Corp history, even back before the name was changed. This was, most certainly, due to just how many superpowered lab techs were involved, and to how much Lena did after hours. Even after her engineers went home, she stayed, because she couldn’t bear to be apart from this project before she’d seen it through. 

She worked like a woman possessed. Balancing half-ton pieces of rebar was nothing on an ordinary day, but consumed by this intense focus, Lena had thrown together the whole rig like she was juggling hollowed-out eggshells - infinitely precise and careful, the only sweat broken was due to mental strain. She had checked and rechecked and re-rechecked her math, and ordinarily, that would have been enough to allay her concerns. She should have been confident. 

She was, in actuality, anything but. 

Lena checked her math twice more than usual because she didn’t want to risk a mistake. She didn’t want to ruin Rhea’s plans. She didn’t want some subconscious itch to keep this magnificent mentor around to stand in the way of doing what was right. Perhaps it was selfish, holding up production to make sure the numbers made sense, but Lena couldn’t help but think it would be more selfish to risk letting a mistake slip through.

Monday morning, bright and early, she was certain she’d done it. She finished her calculations around the start of the workday after a frenetically sleepless night and was so exhausted, all she wanted to do was go home and sleep. It didn’t even register as odd that, when she thought of home, she thought of Kara’s apartment and not her own penthouse, all clean lines and posh asceticism - that’s how tired she was. 

Kara texted, right then. It was a selfie from her desk at CatCo, the prep phase of an article open on her laptop and notes spread out over every available flat surface, aiming finger guns at the camera and winking like a goof, because she was adorable and had better timing than a professional drummer. Lena paused, distracted for a long moment or two by her girlfriend’s face, before sending back a single red heart emoji.

Kara’s immediate gleeful response was asking Lena out for lunch and, at the behest of Lena’s suddenly snarling stomach, she fired back an emphatic yes. There were about four hours until Kara’s lunch break, and four hours was time aplenty to check her math.

Four hours was not time aplenty, as it turned out, and Lena came to that conclusion about fifteen minutes before she was supposed to meet Kara.

 

[11.45a.m.] rain check?

[Kara, 11.45a.m.] of course!! everything ok?

 

Lena smiled, ear to ear, and cradled her phone to her chest. She fired back, reassuring Kara that everything was fine - she was just up to her eyeballs in math. Kara offered to bring something by, and Lena was about to accept; it would be a fantastic opportunity to have a fresh pair of eyes on her work, and to introduce Kara to Rhea, who was still a little iffy on that front since her first introduction to their relationship was less than ideal.

As she was about to type back, Rhea appeared, food in hand. “Your thrall said this was protocol.”

“Thrall?”

“Yes, the tall one.”

“Hector? My assistant.”

“Ah!”

“He stepped in for my previous assistant, Jess, once she joined the Board after… it’s a long story. But I tend to get very focused when I work, often to my own detriment, and she must have given him instructions.” Lena set her phone down and took the box. “Thank you.”

“You’re welcome.” 

And so Lena ended up eating lunch with Rhea, picking over her salad and her math. She finished checking the numbers over, and she felt good about them, and she promptly went to her own apartment and passed the hell out. 

Tuesday, she came into Lab 13 with every intention of handing the math over to the other engineers for a final crowdsourced once-over. Truly. Honestly. 

She showed up, caffeinated and ready to rock, at six in the morning. As she drafted the email, though, she saw a discrepancy. 

Which never happened. Lena didn’t make mistakes in her math - she never had; it was something she took great pride in, something she clung to in her lowest moments of self-esteem.

So, horrified, she deleted the email and retreated to her private lab, hoping that the solitude would facilitate better calculations. Piece by piece, line by line, equation by equation, Lena dug through her numbers. 

And found nothing. 

Nothing. 

There was no mistake. 

“What,” Lena hissed, “the fuck.”

Her phone rang, and she picked it up without looking or thinking, repeating herself into it. 

“Are you okay? What’s going on? Do you - ?”

“Kara! Oh, god, no, no, everything’s - it’s fine, I’m fine, I’m an idiot but I’m fine.” Lena closed her eyes and leaned back onto her bench. “Stay where you are, there’s nothing to worry about.”

“You sound stressed.”

“That’s so accurate.” Lena’s jaw tightened, and she closed her eyes. “But I’m okay. Cross my heart; it’s just been a while since I’ve been on this side of the operation, and my brain’s not cooperating.”

“I trust you.” Kara clacked for a moment, typing furiously with one hand, then said, “I’m distracting you.”

“…yes. I’m sorry - ”

“No, no, don’t be sorry!”

“You’re not doing anything wrong!”

“I get it, i zhor, don’t worry.” More typing noises filtered through, and Lena got the sense that Kara was doing mental calculations of her own. “I’m in the early stages of this article, so I can get away from my desk for a little while if you want me to drop by.”

“You don’t have to do that,” Lena insisted, heart fluttering. “Stay, work on your article.”

I love you.

“You sure?”

“I will spend today ironing things out, and you will work on your article, and when we’re done, we can have the most gigantic lunch.”

“I’m gonna hold you to that,” Kara said, a fondly teasing lilt in her voice. “Let me know when you’re done.”

And Lena, with astonishing lack of foresight, said, “I’ll probably be done by, like, tomorrow.”

“Wednesday. Got it. Now get back to work!”

I love you.

“Yes, dear,” Lena drawled, already feeling more energetic. She hung up, and went back to work. 

Her first check was fine, but the second had a glaring flub that would have ruined everything. The third check, however, revealed no mistakes, and Lena probably would have felt like she was going insane if not for that tiny chat with Kara. As things stood, she was ready to go back to work, and so she did. 

As she ran through the numbers again, pacing back and forth through Lab 13, every line started to blur together. She stopped cold by the patch of concrete she’d poured after Liveware’s visit, setting her tablet down on the workbench, and ripped her hair out of her ponytail, which was swishing over her shoulders and slipping out of place. 

Getting so fixated on her stupid ponytail disobeying was probably a sign that she needed a break, but if Lena had one talent anywhere near as powerful as her mathematic prowess, it was ignoring signs to step back. 

Lena’s hands worked so fast they were probably a blur, tying her hair out of her face, but then her hair band snapped as she stretched it around the base of her bun, and she had to swallow a bubble of the sort of language that wasn’t allowed on basic cable.

Rhea, whose focus had so far been evenly split between Lena and construction supervision, turned all her attention to the former, crossing the lab to Lena’s side. “May I?” 

“Knock yourself out.” 

Out of heels, the two of them were the exact same height, but with Lena in flats, Rhea was tall enough to look down at the top of her head. She, too, made quick work of Lena’s hair, but her efficiency wasn’t so brusque. Her fingers were fast, but they were also painstakingly gentle. Lena’s eyes closed. 

The last time someone braided her hair, it was Kara, benched because of Daxamite assassins. She’d been just as quick and capable, and her touch was warm.

The time before that, though, she’d been four years old and going to pre-school. Marion Smith, six hours out from dying, had felt well enough to carefully plait the top of Lena’s hair back and tie it off with an elastic. 

After that, it took twenty years for someone to make that particular affectionate overture again, and in the interim, Lena got pretty good at braiding her own hair. She got pretty good at taking care of herself. Being taken care of was still something she was working on.

Rhea’s hands in her hair felt nice, it was as simple as that, and not the way Kara’s had. This felt maternal. Though she was standing in her own lab - the lab she had because she was a grown adult, and a scientist, and a competent, if reluctant, businesswoman - she may as well have been sitting on the living room floor of her mother’s Metropolis apartment, the size of a shoebox, feeling peaceful.

“As much as I appreciate your dedication to this project, Lena, you don’t need to run yourself ragged for it.”

“I think I’ve been looking at the numbers for too long,” she admitted, skirting the issue. “I thought I saw a mistake, but when I went and checked, it wasn’t there. I can’t afford to let any mistakes slip through.”

“You have a whole team at your disposal. You’re in charge. Make use of the people you’re leading - delegate.”

Lena huffed a laugh, dropping her head. “I’ve gotten that advice before.”

“You’re a smart girl, and a gifted leader. It’s hard to step back and cede control when you don’t know if things will be executed to your standards.”

“If you want something done right…” Don’t let Lena near it.

“Do it yourself.” With that, Rhea was finished, tucking the tail of Lena’s braid securely away. “I have faith in you, Lena. I know you can get this done. If getting it done means you need to change the way you look at things, or who’s looking at them, so be it. You will figure this out.”

She gave Lena’s shoulders a squeeze, and Lena stood straighter, opening her eyes. “Thank you, Rhea.”

“Of course. Come take a look at construction - give your mind a chance to settle.”

Lena followed Rhea over to the device, nearly complete. The whole thing felt very Star Trek, and if not for the infinite cocoon of red tape surrounding this, and any, L Corp project, she would have wanted to show it to Winn, who would have probably blown a fuse at the very sight of it. Hell, she’d blown a fuse at the specs alone; seeing it, nearly completed and brimming with promise, she felt like she was finally doing something right.

Being Galaxy Girl, she was a hero in a way that Lex could never be. No one would ever think to compare the two. Being Lena Luthor, CEO, however, was a constant comparison. The board members she still had were the ones who wouldn’t dare to connect those dots, the ones who had never met him. 

Still, part of her craved the comparison. Some tiny corner of her heart beat solely for the off chance that the right person would tell her she was just as good as her brother, didn’t dare to dream that she might be better. Jack calling her the best of us didn’t fill that void; Kara’s support and affection didn’t, either, and that in and of itself was monstrous, because how could Kara not be enough?

“Everything’s running smoothly,” said one engineer, offering Lena a glance at their clipboard. “Should be operational by Friday.”

Peering down at the timeline, Lena chirped, “Fantastic,” and tried to sound like she meant it.

Lena worked through the night, infinitesimally slowly. 

Look at it in a new way, she thought, remembering Rhea’s advice. Look at it like a new person.

Once everyone else had gone home for the night - once Rhea had teleported off to wherever she slept - Lena holed up in her private lab again.

Look at it like someone new.

She balanced her tablet on her knees, hunching down around a beaker, running her fingers through the dead swarm. 

“How would you do this, Jacky?” she murmured. “The math was never your favorite part, but you always got it done. You saw answers I missed.”

The swarm was unresponsive, filtering through her fingers. It may as well have been a beaker full of ball bearings, for all the answers it gave her, but it was sort of comforting. 

With a sigh, Lena set the beaker aside and corked it, turning back to her math. “How would Lex do this? The golden boy wouldn’t be lost in his own equations.”

Lena dug through L Corp’s servers, deeper and deeper, until she found her brother’s notes. If she couldn’t figure it out on her own merit, she’d copy him.

Looking at Lex’s notes didn’t make things clearer. In fact, they just made things messy. His handwriting just made her think of the notes he used to leave her, the cards he sent when she was away at school; his projects grew more and more benign the further back she read, and it just made her feel, for a moment, every second of spoiled hope that she might have saved him.

After a while, she gave up on Lex’s notes, on her own notes. She ended up sleeping in her own lab, mulling things over, and when she woke up, she turned back to the numbers with a fresh eye. 

An eye that got things right. The equations balanced out with more power output, and they felt finished. The math checked out. 

“Ms. Luthor?”

“Hector. What’s going on?”

“Your calendar had a lunch set up for you and Ms. Danvers - ”

“Had?”

“It didn’t look like a good time to disturb you, so I - ”

Lena sighed. “Canceled?”

“Was that wrong?”

“No! No, you’re fine, you did fine.” Lena stood, rolling her shoulders. “Can you have something delivered to her office for me?”

“Of course, Ms. Luthor.”

Lena rattled off Kara’s standard Chinese takeout order, as well as a specifically meaningful bouquet - purple hyacinths, geraniums, hydrangeas, and white ivy tendrils - before heading back down to Lab 13. 

Things really took off after that. There was a test field in San Isidro Valley that L Corp had bought up after Lord Industries tanked that was perfect for what Rhea had in mind, and they reallocated the finally finished entry point to the middle of the desert while, back at the lab, Lena inputted the finished algorithm.

“I’m so proud of you, Lena,” Rhea said, standing by her side as they watched everything fall into place.

A smile crept across Lena’s face before she could even think to fight it - one that only widened when, once she left the lab, Hector delivered something from Kara.

The bouquet was barely that - it was a tiny posy of daffodils and nothing else, with the fortune from a fortune cookie attached to the wrapping. The fortune itself read love can turn a cottage into a golden palace, and on the other side, Kara had scribbled a note.

“‘There are lots of meanings for these, but I like this one best: the sun is always shining when I’m with you.’ Oh.” Lena’s cheeks pinked. 

The rest of the note went on to say that Lena cancelling was fine; Kara’s article had reached critical mass, and she was lucky if she could get away from her desk to pee, let alone get lunch, so she appreciated Lena sending food by, and they’d see each other that weekend. 

“Of course, the one time her handwriting isn’t the size of a truck, it looks like an ant wrote it.” Lena clutched the daffodils as tightly as she could without making an idiot of herself. “Have a good night, Hector.”

“You, too, Ms. Luthor.”

As Lena leaned back against the wall, she made an attempt to furtively bury her face in the flowers - one that would have worked, if Rhea hadn’t stepped into the hall. 

“Those are pretty,” she remarked, running her finger along one velvety petal.

“Kara sent them.”

“Oh?”

“I’ve had to cancel on her so many times this week, and she’s been so understanding.” Lena’s shoulders softened. “I can’t wait to introduce you.”

Rhea nodded, plucked the petal, rubbing it between her fingertip and thumb. “I can’t wait to meet her.”

☆

If Kara couldn’t get away from her desk, then Lena would just have to come to her. She stopped off at Noonan’s, because it was close enough that, if her plan didn’t work, it wouldn’t be too obvious that she’d failed, and strode on into CatCo.

There wasn’t any real fuss bringing her in, especially in comparison to the high security at L Corp, and any waiting or obstacles that might have come her way were stymied by three things.

One, she knew the boss.

Two, she’d been here time and time again with Kara.

Three, she was Lena Luthor, oft-editorialized by the very magazine operating out of that building. 

Being notorious did, on occasion, have its perks.

Knowing Kara, right around now, she’d be just about to leave Snapper’s corner of the main floor, which meant Lena would need to rush to actually catch her before she left.

This is going to be fun, she thought. She walked into the stairwell, found it utterly unoccupied, and started to run - not just fast, not just inhumanly fast, but fast enough to test a theory of hers: whether or not a superspeedy alien could move too fast for the human eye to see.

Or, rather, the motion-detecting security camera. There was one planted on every landing, and none of them went off when Lena ran by. She moved fast enough that, after darting through the doors on Kara’s floor, she managed to close the door soundlessly before anyone had even cottoned on to her arrival.

Sure enough, Kara was just ducking out of Snapper’s doors as Lena approached them.

“Hey, sunshine.”

“Lena!” 

Immediately, Kara swept her off her feet into a huge hug, and Lena melted into it. 

“I thought you were - ”

“I figured it out, and I knew you’d be stuck all day, so I thought I’d give being a good girlfriend a shot.”

“Oh, you’re the best girlfriend.” With one last squeeze, Kara unwrapped Lena from her arms and took her hand, lacing their fingers together. “C’mon, let’s go eat on the balcony.”

“Is this the..?”

“No!” Kara nudged her glasses further up her nose. “Different balcony.”

Lena swallowed a laugh and squeezed Kara’s hand. As they strolled off towards the balcony, she shot a look over her shoulder at Snapper, who looked none too pleased to see her.

Good.

Ordinarily, Lena didn’t enjoy people’s slightly fearful disdain towards her, but considering Snapper had fired Kara, and then talked down to her, from him, she welcomed it. 

Only one or two other people were out there, and they were too focused on getting ten minutes away from Snapper to pay either of them any mind. 

Lunch was actually nice. More than nice. It was a welcome reprieve from the admittedly self-induced high stress environment of Lena’s labs, and Kara seemed genuinely happy just to see her, which made Lena feel all the guiltier for skipping out on her.

Kara knew. Of course Kara knew. But Kara artfully skirted around any and all discussions of plan cancelling, at least three steps ahead at all times while dragging Lena through every conversational rosebush in the metaphoric garden, from local elections to ‘their’ dogs to 90s pop, and Lena loved her for it.

“I mean, I love him.”

Lena nodded, thoroughly charmed. 

“I do! I love him,” Kara insisted emphatically, “but come on! JT has got to be the only one holding up a reunion right now.”

“Oh, obviously!” Lena grinned, puckish, and arched an eyebrow before going in for the kill. “Here, but let me ask you this, right? Would you rather have an *NSYNC reunion or JT and Britney back together?”

“Ugh!” Kara clasped her hands to her chest. “My OTP!”

Lena giggled, just soaking up her sunshiny girlfriend’s easy exuberance. 

“That is an impossible question - ”

“Yeah?”

“ - and you are cruel for asking!”

“Well, you know, sometimes my Luthor genes just…” Lena gave a blasé shrug, deliberate in her coolness despite Lex’s notes still fresh in her head. “Shine through!”

Mission accomplished.Kara laughed, uproarious, and any reluctance Lena may have had to make that joke disappeared, burned off by her bright, hiccuppy laughter. Lena started laughing, too, swept up in the relief.

Kara reached across the table and took her hand as their giggling petered out. “Thank you for catching lunch with me.”

“Yeah, well…” Lena tried to remain cool and unaffected, and most likely failed. “Since I cancelled the last three times, and you said you couldn’t get away, I figured you were worth the extra effort.”

“Yeah,” said Kara carefully, “what’s keeping you so busy?”

“It’s top secret.”

“Intriguing.”

Lena’s cheeks warmed, and she promised, “As soon as I can tell anyone anything, you’ll get an exclusive.”

Kara beamed, tilting her head to the side and raising her eyebrows, sliding her glasses down her nose - it was a very compelling face.

“I’m working with a new partner,” Lena admitted.

Kara hummed encouragingly, and it didn’t feel like she was prying for information - she was just happy for Lena, and supporting her, and the most amazing girlfriend.

“Yeah, she’s - she’s fantastic. It’s… It’s like having a mentor, you know? You’ll love her.” Lena smiled crookedly, laying her hand overtop of Kara’s, running her thumb over the ridge of her knuckles. “Promise.”

“You’ve got to give me something,” Kara begged, “I have to have something to look forward to!”

“What do you know,” Lena started slowly, “about quantum entanglement?”

“Quantum what?”

A hair flustered, Lena pressed on, tripping over her own tongue: “Polyatomic anions?”

Kara pulled the most excessively befuddled face, and Lena knew she was being messed with.

“I know you know what I’m talking about!” she hissed, eyes wide.

Eyes wide, Kara said, “Negative,” and Lena pulled a face at the atrocious pun, which just made Kara laugh again.

“Well, when you see what we’re doing, you’ll get it, I’m sure. It’ll probably be dreadfully boring.”

“I am positive that it will blow me away.”

Lena, blushing red from head to toe, was very tempted to lean over and kiss Kara. If not for the fact that they were at her office, and they hadn’t actually talked about that boundary, she might have. 

That, and the infortuitous buzz of her phone.

“Oh! Actually, this is her.” Lena started out of her chair, albeit reluctantly. “I’m gonna have to go, because we’re doing our first test today.”

Kara rose to her feet and leaned over the table, pulling Lena into a perfect hug. “Oh, it was so good to see you.”

Lena tucked her face into Kara’s shoulder under the guise of a nod, holding a little tighter. 

“Next time, lunch is on me.”

Of course, things couldn’t be so easy. 

Lena answered Rhea’s call in the stairwell, walking at a thoroughly normal pace, and ended up sprinting out of the building just to burn off the swell of impotent anxiety in her chest. This test would quell it for good, she was certain.

Except it didn’t.

The structures couldn’t handle the energy output, shorting out almost catastrophically on the first go. Which meant her math was wrong. 

Worse still, the aftermath was interrupted by another call - this one from Kara. Apparently, while things had gone to hell in her lab, they’d gone to hell in Simmons Square, too. An alien with psychic powers had gone berserk, started throwing cars, caused thousands of dollars of property damage. The news was painting an ugly picture, and the DEO had her out patrolling, looking for the Phorian.

“Do they need me to come in?”

“That’s usually why they make these phone calls,” Kara said. “What’s going on?”

“I just…” Lena looked around her lab, at her failures lingering, smoky, in the air. “Am I even allowed? I thought I was still benched.”

“They didn’t call you?”

“No.”

“I’ll - shoot. I’ll talk to Alex.”

“No, it’s fine. I’m - ” Lena sighed. “I’m busy here. Cleanup.”

“Cleanup?”

“I… miscalculated.”

“Oh, Lena.”

“It’s fine! It’s fine, I’m working on it - we’re working on it.”

“I can look at the numbers with you, later. If you want!”

“What happened to ‘quantum wha..?’” Lena teased.

“I was doing calculus at age four.” Kara at least had the decency to sound sheepish. “I can swing by L Corp after work, bring by dinner.”

“Or I could come over?”

“Sounds great. See you then.”

“Bye.”

Lena resisted going to Paka’s with Rhea at first, because Kara was going to bring her dinner, but Kara was also searching one of the largest population centers in the country for someone who didn’t want to be found, and Rhea was difficult to say no to.

Not that she pressured Lena into anything - and wasn’t that a first? - but because every suggestion she made was one Lena would have made herself, and because spending time with Rhea was nice. 

Plus, Rhea had offered, “Just drinks, then? I wouldn’t want to tread on your time with your girlfriend,” and that was just the thing Lena needed to hear to assuage any guilt she might have felt about making overlapping plans.

So, before heading out with Rhea to collaboratively pretend they could get drunk off the drinks menu at a human restaurant, Lena sent Kara a text explaining things.

As Kara read the message, Lena typed, deleted, and retyped the same sixteen words - you could come inside and meet Rhea and we can all go over the math together - because Rhea and Kara were both brilliant, strong women who, against all odds, liked her, and if anyone could fix her miscalculations, it was the two of them. 

On her fourth iteration of deleting the same message, Kara texted Lena back, so she gave up on the offer and read Kara’s response: i can swing by and pick u up?

Lena shot back a single red heart, followed by the address, then headed out with Rhea. 

The atmosphere was elegantly relaxed as always, but it did nothing to soothe her frayed nerves, nor to distract her from the notes on her tablet, which she’d only brought with her with the intent of sharing it with Kara.

Seated at the bar beside her, Rhea reached over and gently turned the tablet face-down by laying her hand overtop of Lena’s. “Today was just our first test. You can’t expect it to be perfect on the first attempt.”

“I quadruple-checked my calculations on this, okay? The reaction of the polyatomic anions was supposed to be strong enough to spark the core of the generator.”

With boundless patience in her low, rich voice, Rhea said, “Neither of us has gotten to where we are without persistence,” but for once, it didn’t work.

“If I can’t make this work, we won’t - ” Lena paused, running her fingertip up and down the stem of her wineglass and glancing around the restaurant before continuing at a whisper. “We won’t be able to power the portal. This was supposed to revolutionize the way everything was transported - eliminate famine, the need for fossil fuels!” She sighed, glancing over at Rhea with unguarded eyes. “I wanted to help my planet. And get you home to yours.”

“And you will,” Rhea murmured, laying her hands over Lena’s shoulders and squeezing fondly. “You’re making advancements in science that most people on Earth could not even dream of! No one said it would be easy.”

Lena’s head drooped. “What if I can’t make it work? What if I can’t get you home?”

“I have confidence in you, Lena.”

There was that strange drawl on her name again, that drag between the first consonant and vowel - like in the way J’onn and M’gann’s  names were pronounced. Someday, Lena would ask her why.

Rhea hopped down from her stool, hands still on Lena’s shoulders. “I am going to the test facility to check the progress of the portal.” Her fingertips glided across Lena’s back, one hand coming up to cup her chin with infinite tenderness. “I know you don’t believe it yet, but you’re going to make this work.”

Lena smiled, helpless to stop herself, and fired off a text.

Not two seconds later, an usher approached Lena. “Um, there’s someone for you. Out back?”

“Oh?” Lena picked up her wineglass by the step and swirled it coyly. “Who is it?”

“Um. Supergirl?”

“I’ll be right out.”

Lena settled the check, tipping absurdly well even by her own standards for two glasses of wine, one unfinished, and strolled out to meet her girlfriend.

“You’re so dramatic,” she purred, draping her arms around Kara’s neck. 

“You sent me something I’m pretty sure I’ve seen on Straight White Boys Texting - ‘hey babe u up?’” Kara scoffed fondly and wrapped her arms around Lena’s waist. “How else was I supposed to respond?”

“I thought it was funny. Since, you know, you’ve been flying around all day - which, by the way, how did you get away from Snapper?”

“I may be bad for your productivity, but seeing you is great for mine.”

Lena thanked the Frenchman with feelings of inadequacy who’d invented the high heel, and didn’t even have to stretch up or pull Kara down to kiss her. 

“You,” she murmured, “are very sweet.”

Kara beamed, megawatt, and kissed her forehead. “Come on. Up, up, and away.”

“Am I racing you?”

“In those shoes?”

Lena arched an eyebrow, then stepped out of her shoes. The asphalt of the alleyway behind Paka’s was, thankfully, not as disgusting as some alleyway asphalt, but it was still a weird sensation, and she wiggled her toes to get used to it as she bent down to pick up her heels. “On your mark…”

“Get set…”

They leapt upwards at the same time, twin blurs across the National City skyline. Lena couldn’t quite make her brain turn off all the way, but she did come close, the wind whipping past her cheeks, her bare feet whispering over rooftops. 

Kara had the advantage of being able to take the most direct route, as the crow (or Kryptonian) flies, but Lena was stubborn, off the clock, and desperately in need of a win. She threw herself through a cracked-open hallway window, ricocheting up the stairs, and opened Kara’s unlocked front door, bursting into the kitchen as Kara shot through the living room window.

“Tie?”

“You’d look nice in one.”

Kara laughed, flinging her arms around Lena’s waist and twirling on her tiptoes before flopping back onto the couch. Lena grinned, knocking her forehead into Kara’s collarbone.

“You’ve gotten faster,” Kara remarked. “Way faster. Have you - never mind.”

“What? Been sunbathing naked?”

“Not even remotely what I was going to ask you, but okay, sure. Have you?”

“I’ve been buried in my own lab. The last time I saw the sun was lunch with you.”

“Well,” Kara said, planting a kiss on Lena’s hair, “then I’m doubly glad you came.”

Lena let out a breath, tension oozing out of her body, but that state of pseudo-relaxation didn’t last long. Soon, she sat up, whipping out her tablet and thrusting her calculations into Kara’s face. “Tell me where I fucked up.”

“This is your math?”

“Yes.”

“It doesn’t - this looks like - ”

Lena snatched the tablet back. “I looked over Lex’s notes. Tried to get a feel for how he would have done it.”

“Lena…”

Kara sat up, draping herself over Lena’s shoulder, running her fingers through her hair. 

“This needs to go well, Kara. I need to do this right. There’s so much riding on this project, and - ”

“Hey, hey, it’s okay,” Kara murmured. “You’re going to get it. You always do. You’re a genius - ”

“Says the girl who was doing calculus at age four.”

“ - even by Kryptonian standards.”

Something caught in Lena’s throat. “Really?”

“Yeah. You would’ve blown the Science Guild away.”

“Oh.”

Kara kissed the hinge of Lena’s jaw, then opened her palm, silently requesting the equations again. Lena, melting, passed them over and closed her eyes. 

“This is a lot of power output,” Kara said after a minute, “but it’s all being wasted. The generator can’t keep up.”

“Tell me about it,” Lena grumbled, “but my math was - it stopped making sense to me. And it was my math!”

“Can I look at that?”

“Yeah, sure.” Lena flicked through the files on that tablet until she found her own numbers, then passed it back. “Ta-da.”

“These are brilliant.”

“Find the mistake.”

Kara’s brow furrowed, but ever diligent, she hunted for an error. Finally, she gave up, sighing, “If there’s a mistake in here, I can’t find it.”

“Neither can I, not consistently, which is the problem.” Lena slumped, knocking her brow bone into Kara’s cheek. “If there is a mistake that I don’t catch, and things go wrong, people could get hurt. If there isn’t a mistake, but I fabricate one to correct, the equation will be unbalanced, the algorithm won’t work, and people - ”

“Could get hurt.” Kara gave Lena’s shoulder a good knead, mulling things over. “You need a night off.”

“I can’t take a night off.”

“Yes, you can. Come patrolling with me. See if we can’t find this Phorian.”

“I’m not allowed. I’m still benched, remember?”

“Well, screw that!” 

Lena laughed.

“Suit up, Galaxy Girl. You need to give your brain a break so, tomorrow, you can look at your equations with fresh eyes and get this done.”

“Fine.” Lena stood, then pulled Kara to her feet. “You’re just lucky I left it here.”

Along with all my cute underwear. And basically everything in my bathroom. And my favorite coffee cup.

She shed her skirt and blouse like old skin, wondering when pulling on armor-plated spandex had gotten so easy to do. Kara braided her hair up, and it was so recently familiar a gesture that questions Lena wanted to ask Rhea started bubbling up.

“Hey. Does my name mean anything?”

“Um, in English? Not really, but there are plenty of names that it’s short for from other languages, Greek, Gaelic, that have - ”

“No, in - ” Lena swallowed. “Languages from other planets?”

“Well, on Krypton, inah means…”

“What?”

Quietly, Kara said, “Daughter.”

“Oh, Kara, I’m so - ”

“No, it’s all good.” 

Lena could practically hear her smiling. 

“But your name, in particular? No.”

☆

A few hours into their patrol, Kara stopped dead midair, alighting gently on a rooftop to answer a phone call. Lena, a block ahead, pivoted on her toes and leapt back to meet her.

“Uh-huh. Okay. Do you need me to come in?”

Who is it? Lena mouthed.

Kara mouthed back Alex, then said, “And he’s okay with that?” After a moment, she shrugged, hooking the fingers of one hand through the opposite elbow - as close to crossing her arms as she could get holding a phone to her ear. “Does J’onn want to end the search?”

Lena, whose hearing had been sharper than usual that past week, had worked so hard to not passively eavesdrop on everything around her that it was hard work to even consider it now. So she didn’t.

“Okay. Bye.” Kara hung up, tucking her phone into her pocket, and sighed. “Search is off. James got a lead while he was out Guardian-ing. Apparently, the Phorian who attacked in the park today has a kid.”

“Oh. Wow.”

“And he likes James, so James is going to take him to work tomorrow, talk to him outside of an interrogation room, see if he can get anything out of him.”

Lena couldn’t help but feel a little bitter that James, who wasn’t even a DEO contractor, got to be an official Director-approved part of this, while she had to tag along on patrol.

As if she hadn’t noticed Kara carefully avoiding mention of her presence.

The adrenaline, the endorphins, the hedonistic joy of just going full tilt with all her powers and focusing solely on the physical, it all dissipated. 

“Hey.” Kara reached out and took her hand, skin warm even through the armor. “Wanna just go fight regular old human crime, instead?”

“No, I should - I should just go to the test site. Do some work.”

“Lena, wait.”

Lena waited. 

Kara stepped in close and cradled the line of her jaw, ducking down to kiss her softly. “Wanna watch the sun rise at my place?”

“Sunrise isn’t for another six hours.”

“I’m sure we can figure out something to distract ourselves for that long.”

Adrenaline. Endorphins. Hedonistic pleasure. Kara’s perfect coffee.

Lena smiled crookedly. “I wouldn’t put it past us.”

☆

Admittedly, Lena did feel better in the morning, a warm calm settled over her bone-deep as she wrapped Kara’s sheet around herself and wandered into the kitchen.

Kara smiled over two coffee cups - one of which was, indeed, Lena’s own - as soon as Lena’s feet hit the floor and passed one her way. “Good morning.”

“Morning, sunshine.”

Kara, somehow, smiled wider, draping herself along Lena’s bare back and turning them both towards the window. They both stayed like that, wrapped up in each other, as they watched the sun rise.

Once it was up, Lena felt a rush of energy that had absolutely nothing to do with the caffeine. “I need to shower.”

“Go ahead. Your shampoo and everything is in there.”

Lena drained the last of her cup and kissed Kara’s cheek before zipping off to wash her hair. Despite the presence of her own lush spa-brand toiletries, she ended up smelling like Kara’s stuff instead, wondering if four-ish months of being together was too soon to move in.

“You,” Kara said, buttoning her shirt up over her crest, “don’t have any work clothes here. Except for what you wore last night.”

“Crap.”

“You could borrow a pair of my pants.”

“We don’t wear the same size.”

“True.” Kara stood, shirt still half open, and crossed to her closet, which she flung open to reveal a stunning array of khakis. “When I’m not wearing something under them.”

Lena grinned, waiting for Kara to hear her own unintentional innuendo and absolutely eating up the sight of her in, quite possibly, the softest butch outfit she’d ever worn. The shirt was pink, and plaid, and Lena was in love.

“Not like that! I meant, I tuck my cape into my pants, so I have to size up.” Kara pulled out a hanger with a pair of black work pants folded neatly over the bar and presented it to Lena proudly. “Look! It won’t even disrupt your aesthetic.”

I love you.

Lena kissed Kara’s cheek and took the pants. Sure enough, they fit, and she did find one of her own silk blouses hiding under all the underwear she’d left behind, so the final result wasn’t too big a departure from her usual work standard. “How do I look?”

“Wonderful.”

Lena beamed and finished buttoning up Kara’s shirt for her, using it as an excuse to pull her down by the collar and give her a proper good morning kiss. “I have to get going. San Isidro Valley waits for no woman.”

“Bye,” Kara said, half-laughing.

Of course, even so nice a morning - or night before - couldn’t form an adequate buffer for another day’s failure. Not even a full day’s failure, either, because it wasn’t even noon when they managed to fry the portal.

Again.

“Still isn't working?” Rhea asked. 

Lena crossed her arms, feeling far too petulant. “Was it me throwing it down in disgust or the sparks that gave it away?” 

Turning towards the two engineers standing by them, Rhea said, “Can you give us a minute?” and waited until they’d skedaddled to continue speaking. She didn’t have to wait long; something about her just radiated power, and no one dared to disobey her. It was impressive. She put a hand on Lena’s back and, with the air of a stateswoman, said, “Failure is a part of the process, Lena. I told you this was going to take time.”

“It's not about time. I'm just not getting it.” Acerbic, Lena swished her ponytail, saying, “You know, maybe we should pay a visit to Stryker Island. Get Lex Luthor to come in and save the day.”

“You think he could get this working?” 

Lena’s heart sank. Even Rhea had lost faith. “Lex was the genius who was supposed to save the world.” She quickly looked away from her mentor and towards the portal. “You know, I - I just thought that, if I could make this work, I could prove to the world, and to my mother that I was as good as the golden boy. That I wasn’t a liability, or in need of repair.” Lena shook her head slowly. “I think, most of all, I just wanted to prove it to myself.”

“You don’t have to prove anything,” said Rhea, emphatic, insistent. “You’re smarter than Lex.”

Laughing, Lena shook her head.

“No. I’m not saying that to make you feel better, I’m saying it as a scientist. As someone who knows.” Rhea turned towards the portal, too, giving Lena the chance to sneak surreptitious glances her way. “But you need to stop thinking like your brother.

“From what you’ve told me about him, he’s a man who is concerned with power. And that’s how you’ve been trying to fix this: give it more power, you think it will work.”

“Yeah, but it just keeps blowing.”

“But you’re not a person who’s concerned with power,” Rhea said, finally catching Lena in the act and holding her gaze, touching her arm. “Are you?”

Lena found herself smiling.

“So, if you weren’t trying to do what Lex would do, what would you do?”

“I’d try to find a way to increase the anion input without overloading the energy output.”

“Not power,” said Rhea, eyes burning bright. “Balance.”

And everything clicked into place. Kara’s advice and Rhea’s were the same, fundamentally, and Lena’s head was clear and refreshed enough that maybe, just maybe, she’d be able to see her own equations correctly. 

She had work to do, and as she sat down to do it, Lena felt supercharged. Her fingers were a blur on the keys, matching pace with her brain, as she wrote an all new algorithm for the portal’s systems. She glanced over her shoulder, finally finished, and saw Rhea hovering behind her, looking at her the way Eliza looked at Kara or Alex. She felt good.

“If my mother,” she said, voice bright as she pushed up out of her seat, “had given me pep-talks like you, imagine the things I could’ve done.”

A shadow crossed behind Rhea’s eyes, and but it didn’t dim her. “I’m happy to have mused you. But, trust me, it isn’t always easy being the parents we aspire to be.” She looked at Lena, all fire, and asked, “Shall we test it again?”

“Let me just plug in the algorithm and fire it up.” 

Lena raced over to the mainframe, too excited to moderate her speed. She glanced over her shoulder, just once, to look at Rhea as she looked out at the portal - at her way home. 

I can’t ask her to take a seat on the board, she decided. I won’t. The way she looks at that portal… only a monster could ask her to leave all that behind.

Once the algorithm was operating, Lena switched controls to a tablet and marched over to stand with Rhea.

“Here goes nothin’.”

The generator whirred; the portal lit up. Lena’s eyes flittered from screen to window, surveying both halves of the project at once, heart pounding delightedly.

“Power is running smoothly to the core,” she said, voice somehow perfectly calm despite the fact that, on the inside, she was jumping through the stratosphere with joy. “Anions are reacting at a steady rate.” She dragged the toggles on her screen down, slowly shutting the portal down, before allowing an easy grin to melt across her face.

Rhea, voice impossibly soft, said, “It’s working.”

And it was. 

“We did it!”

“You did it.”

☆

With the portal in perfect working order, technically, Lena’s job was done. Sure, there was scheduling, making certain that it was viable for transport, but, technically? Yeah, she was finished.

But Lena only dealt in technicalities when those technicalities didn’t stand in the way of her helping the people she cared about, so, with the smell of ozone thick in the air, Lena was setting about organizing resources that might help Rhea restore her planet. Ways to help even out the gravitational field, artificial terraforming, agricultural stores and supplies. So absorbed was she in this work, easily the least intellectually taxing project she’d set out to accomplish in the past week, that she didn’t even notice her phone going off at first. Only when she’d reached the end of a bullet point did it strike her as odd that it hadn’t just rung out.

She turned, glancing across the room towards it, and saw Rhea setting it down. “Was that my phone?”

“Telemarketer,” responded Rhea dryly, and Lena found a lump in her throat that hadn’t been there moments before.

Rhea had been on Earth long enough to not only figure out what a telemarketer was, but to develop the same tired disdain for them that every other earthling had. 

And now she was as good as gone.

Lena minimized the note and walked over to Rhea’s side, staring out at the portal with her. 

“Tomorrow we can begin the material trials,” she offered, but there was a wistfulness in Rhea’s eyes that she couldn’t work around. She let out a sigh. “I keep forgetting that success means you’re leaving.Working with you has meant so much to me.”

“Me, too.” Rhea turned to face her, and reached for her hand. “Whatever happens next, I want you to remember never to doubt yourself again. You are a marvel, Lena, and I am so proud to call you my daughter.”

Lena blinked, mouth opening of its own accord to ask why, but Rhea wasn’t answering questions. The hand on Lena’s slipped away, and with it, the tablet with the controls.

“Wait. Wait, what are you - what are you doing?”

Rhea turned away from her, cranking the portal up to its fullest extent, and Lena didn’t bother grabbing for the tablet. She crossed the lab in seconds, opening up the desktop controls, which proved utterly useless.

“Why won’t it shut down? What did you do?”

“What I had to do,” said Rhea calmly. “For our people.”

“Our?”

“Do you want to know what your name means, Lena? In our language?” She smiled, wide and soft. “Daughter. My daughter.”

“I’m not Kryptonian. I - we checked.”

“And thank the gods for that. We share a root language, like we share a solar system, but our languages evolved separately.” Rhea laid a hand on Lena’s, smiling still. “I’m so glad I’ve found you, l’inah.”

The roof of the test facility’s lab caved under the weight of two superpowered aliens, and Lena whipped around to see Kara, suited up, and J’onn still in his human disguise. 

“Turn it off!”

“I can’t.”

“Why won’t it turn off?” he asked.

“I don’t know. She must’ve made it self sustaining somehow.” Lena turned back to Rhea, hands clenched into tight fists at her sides. “What did you do, Rhea?”

Rhea’s smile only widened, and her fingers only curled tighter around a shoulder Lena was too stunned to pull away. “You’ll see.”

Kara launched herself across the lab, tackling Rhea away from a paralyzed Lena and slamming her into a thankfully cosmetic support beam. When J’onn came over to help restrain her, though, it gave Rhea enough of a chance to pull away, to kick him square in the gut and send him flying while pinning Kara to the column with one forearm across her chest.

When she drew back to punch Kara in the face, though, whatever horrible fear inside Lena had frozen her burned off, and Lena grabbed Rhea by the elbow, dragging her off. 

“You,” she spat, “don’t get to touch her.”

“I understand, l’inah. Of course you’d protect the Kryptonian girl who bewitched you, your only window to the stars. But now you have me. We can go home. Together.”

J’onn made it onto his feet only after Kara took off, zooming out towards the portal. “No one messes with my family.”

Rhea reached into her pocket and pulled out a device - round, perfectly fitted to her palm - that glowed with red light. 

Lena lunged for it, but Rhea managed to twist away, reversing the grip Lena had on her arm so, now, Rhea had all the control.

“What is that?”

“A White Martian gave me this. They developed this technology to keep the Greens under their control. It traps a Martian in his own mind.A never-ending nightmare.” Rhea smiled. “Pretty savvy, if you ask me.”

J’onn dropped to his knees, and Lena struggled, however ineffectually, against Rhea’s hold. Then she remembered the last time she’d seen a red light, the last time her mother - god, Rhea was her mother - had her against her will. 

She went slack, a dead weight, and dragged Rhea so far off balance that she managed to pin her to the floor, knocking the device out of her hand. 

“You don’t really want to hurt me,” Rhea said, somehow still totally unflappable. For all that Lena had envied that about her when they’d first met, now, it just made her angry. “Think of what you wanted to do with my portal, l’inah. Helping these sad, pathetic - ”

“Shut up.”

“You’re a hero of Earth,” she continued, “and a hero wouldn’t kill her own mother.”

“You’re not my mother. My mother - my mother’s name was Marion Smith. She was an engineer.”

“Marion Smith was an engineer, yes, but she wasn’t your mother. She was a human woman, perhaps braver and smarter than most, which is why I chose her to look after you.” Rhea smiled. “Well, that and her lover. Lionel Luthor, the smartest man on Earth - and the wealthiest, too. The only one equipped to give you anything resembling the childhood I could have given you if the Kryptonians hadn’t destroyed our world.

“Even though I had to leave you here, I love you. My affection for you is real.”

Lena shook her head dumbly.

“L’inah, you are not going to kill me. Whatever you think of me, I’m still your mother.” Rhea moved, shifting her hands as if to push herself into a seated position, and Lena pushed down, slamming her back into the concrete floors. “We were not the only ones to escape the destruction of our planet. Thousands of Daxamites survived.”

And that - one little word - was enough to suck the fight out of Lena, clean out of her marrow. 

She was what Kara hated more than anything. She was descended from this, from the woman who had trapped J’onn in a nightmare, who had threatened to kill Kara, who had owned slaves.

It was worse than just being a Luthor. Luthors were schoolyard bullies in comparison to the other half of her family tree.

Rhea shot up and pressed something to the back of Lena’s neck, and there was a sharp flare of pain - blinding, worse than any migraine she’d ever had, worse than all of them combined.

Her brain shorted out like the portal had on Lex-like calculations, and Lena’s last thought was that he’d almost saved her.

Maybe he’s not the worst brother in the universe after all.

Notes for the Chapter:

SO! Who saw that coming? Everyone? Was it everyone? Cool.

Lena's bouquet meant "I'm sorry, I'm an idiot, thank you for understanding. I just want to make you happy." :)

That, plus my French teacher is an actual garbage monster (on the inside), and I had a choir performance, and my dad came to visit, and nobody actually gives a fig about any of that, but suffice it to say, there aren't many chapters left in this. I was going to split 21 and 22 into pieces, because there's going to be a lot of stuff going on, but at this point, I think I might just squish everything into the same number of chapters as episodes and then make Chapter 24 everyone's life being significantly better after the invasion is over, and also, Lena and Kara getting their day at the beach.
