21. Chapter 21

Summary for the Chapter:

Takes place during 2x21: Resist. What's a girl to do the third time she'd been kidnapped by a maternal figure, but the first time she's been made the figurehead of space fascists?

Notes for the Chapter:

Warning: Towards the end, Lena has a panic attack, which, understandable. There's a very brief moment in that panic attack that's sort of... Suicidal Lite? So, if suicidal thoughts are a problem for you, skip from "Things on spaceships don't usually do that, not in private quarters" to "But it wasn't that. It was too rhythmic, too insistent." It's just one paragraph, but it's still there. Put yourself first.

Lena would have liked to wake up and have forgotten, if just for a moment. Waking up and wondering why Kara’s bedsheets were so silky, why she wasn’t being actively spooned, would have been a nice two second reprieve. 

But she wasn’t so lucky. She woke up, and she remembered everything. 

“Hello, l’inah.”

Lena batted Rhea’s hand away and shot across the room, putting as much distance between herself and her mother - Jesus, her mother - as possible. “Where the hell am I?” she asked sharply, the fighting stance she assumed more defense than defensive position.

“We’re on our ship. I’ve been taking care of you since Supergirl attacked our portal.”

“Since you knocked me out.” Lena touched the back of her neck self-consciously. “How did you do that?”

“That, my dear, is a very long story.”

“I doubt you’re going to let me go any time soon, so you’ve got time to tell it.” 

Rhea sighed, folding her hands delicately in her lap and remaining perched on the side of the bed. “When you were born, I embedded in you a sort of dampener. Right there, at the nape of your neck. It suppresses your gene expression, your powers. I have a remote control for it that allows me to control the rate of suppression. I knocked you out by overloading the circuits.”

“You… fried my nervous system?”

“Of course. You have more exposure to this system’s yellow sun than I do, and I didn’t have time to convince you on the surface.”

“You could have killed me.”

“I would never take that risk, l’inah.”

A sickly chill ran down Lena’s spine. “Don’t call me that.”

“Why not?”

“It’s not even a name,” Lena spat. “I’m a person, not something you can possess, or own, or control.”

Delicately, Rhea laughed. “Personhood and possession aren’t so diametrically opposed as you might think.”

Lena shuddered. 

“But if you insist!” Smiling, Rhea made a ceding sort of gesture before returning to her neutral posture. “What do you want me to call you?”

“Don’t call me anything.” Lena ripped her hand away from the back of her neck and stood as tall as she could in bare feet, sharp jaw jutting. “You don’t get to call me anything. You lied to me, and used me.”

“I did what I had to do,” Rhea said, firm, decisive. “For our people.”

“Your people.”

“Our people.” Rhea stood, pushing up off the mattress with no real effort - it was such a gesture, such a put-upon mother move, that Lena immediately resumed her position, snatching a lamp up from the nearest bedside table and brandishing it like one of her batons - before rounding the bed, unconcerned. “I meant what I said on the ground. You are a marvel. Even without the advancements of our home, you are the brightest technological mind I have ever encountered, and I know that you are meant for bigger things, better things. This is a planet of wasted potential, and you represent the best it could ever offer. I’m going to make it worthy of you.”

She grabbed Lena’s shoulders, hands horrific in their gentleness, and guided her towards the window. Lena couldn’t understand why she wasn’t fighting back, why she wasn’t swinging that lamp at Rhea’s head and clobbering her like any other criminal. 

Then she looked out, out at the home she’d made for herself, besieged by the very ship that held her, and dropped the lamp, which shattered at her feet. 

“So get comfortable,” Rhea said, rubbing her arms. “You are where you belong, beside me, presiding over this new world that we will create together.”

Lena pulled out of her hands, moving towards the windows with the faltering steps of a baby deer. “There are people down there,” she said, half-amazed and half-aghast. “You’re hurting them.”

“They’re resisting.” Rhea strode silently to meet her, laying her possessive hands on Lena’s back. “Unfortunate, isn’t it? If they would only allow themselves to be ruled, there would be no casualties.”

Lena pressed a trembling hand to her mouth, throat tight. 

“But you, my dear… You can save them. Stop the bloodshed.” Rhea ran her fingers through Lena’s hair, tucking a lock behind her ear, fingertips trailing down the line of her throat and skimming over her erratically pounding pulse point. “Is that something you’d like to do?”

Closing her eyes, concentrating, Lena listened out for the sounds of National City, miles below her. Screaming, screaming, so much screaming. “If I do as you say… you’ll stop hurting them?”

Someone was hit by a blast; Lena could hear them sizzle. 

“Yes. Now, come with me.”

Lena opened her eyes, jaw set, and saw that Rhea was offering her a hand. Unwilling and half-numb, she took it, stepping over broken glass to follow her mother through the ship, muscle memory making her scan her surroundings and catalogue everything she saw - possible weaknesses, points of exit. 

She didn’t think she’d be using them.

They stopped, after mere moments, in an antechamber just off the throne room. Inside was Lena’s bag, and two women in plain shifts, hands clasped in front of them, eyes down. Rhea snapped her fingers, and they picked it up, carrying it to her before kneeling, resting it over both of their thighs, and opening it for her. 

“My - my suit?”

“Galaxy Girl is a symbol that National City believes in,” Rhea said, stroking her hair where it spilled down her back. “Speak to them. Tell your story. The fighting will stop. Everyone will find peace.”

Lena reached for her bag, full of fits and stops, before finally snatching the handles and clutching it to her chest. Eyes down, she murmured, “Thank you,” to the two women, whose heads dropped impossibly lower before they stood, resuming their prior posture and position. For a moment, she waited - for Rhea to say something, to leave - before realizing that wasn’t going to happen. Not on its own, anyway. “If I’m going to change clothes, you need to leave.”

“I removed you from the birthing matrix myself. I dressed you upon arrival. It’s nothing I haven’t seen before.” Her hand felt impossibly heavy on Lena’s back. “I am your mother.”

“I am twenty four years old. Mothers don’t dress their children, not when they’re fully grown.”

“If you insist!” Rhea’s hand lifted. “But be quick. There were four million humans occupying National City when our subjects arrived. I’d hate for that number to dip too low for your liking.”

She left the room, doors whispering shut behind her, and then Lena was left alone with the two women. 

“If you could.” She swallowed hard, throat clicking. “I’m sorry, but could you please look away?”

“Yes, Your Highness.”

Lena considered, very briefly, whether or not her suit’s marionite knuckledusters could punch through the window (yes) and how quickly she could gather up everyone being held there against their will (not quickly enough). Her limbs felt leaden as she tried to find her way out of the dress Rhea had put her in. 

While she was sleeping. 

Eventually, finding no way out of it, she ripped the thing down the back, peeling it off around her ribs, face neutral. At least she’d been left her underwear. Then Lena stepped into her suit. Her  hair wouldn’t cooperate, wouldn’t lie flat under her cowl, and it was the tiniest, pettiest frustration against the big picture - even against the smaller picture of that room, her and two enslaved women, all trapped. 

No. Not trapped. The way they’re forced to be here and the way I’m forced to be here are different. 

Lena knelt, digging through her bag for a hair band or a bobby pin or something, and found nothing she’d been looking for. She did, though, find a tiny piece of metal, no bigger than a ball bearing. 

One of Jack’s bots. 

She pulled it out of the bag, her own clothes and bits of paper skimming the back of her wrist. It looked smaller than ever in her palm, and Lena curled her fingers over it, turning her hand so she didn’t even have to look its way. A piece of paper had managed to get stuck in the armor plating on her arm, and she plucked it free. 

Love can make a cottage into a golden castle.

Swallowing the lump in her throat, Lena tucked both things into her pocket and stood, wiping her eyes. “Thank you. Both of you. You may turn around now.”

Simultaneously, as if being pulled by puppet strings, both women turned. Lena itched to look at them and, on impulse, approached them as slowly as if they were injured strays. “Are either of you injured?”

“No, Your Highness.” There was a skittish intensity in their voices, in their taut shoulders. “All is well.”

“Please speak honestly. I just - ” Lena ran her fingers through her hair, jaw tight. “I need to understand how Rhea… behaves.”

“Our Queen is a good ruler, and powerful.”

Slowly, Lena nodded. Their fear was answer enough. 

With that, she strode out into the throne room and found Rhea standing there, peering out at the city below, with Mon-El. 

“Focus,” Rhea ordered, “on your future.”

“What do you need me for?” he asked, arms flung wide. Over his shoulder, he caught sight of Lena and his jaw pulsed. “You have her.”

“You chose to be here, Mon-El.” Rhea looked tired - of him, of that argument. “If you want to choose to be somewhere else, you are free to make that choice, but there is no guarantee that, amongst all the squabbling on the surface, you won’t be harmed.”

That was enough to quieten him down, and Lena took a step closer. “I’m ready.”

Rhea smiled, then, wide and warm, and Lena put her hands on her hips, feeling the paper crinkle in her pocket. “Let me at least get your hair out of your face.” 

Mon-El rolled his eyes, leaning against the windows like a sullen teenager against the walls of a high school, and Lena wondered if she’d ever made that face when Lillian cosseted Lex in front of her. 

“Come,” Rhea said, “sit.” She swept an arm towards one of three thrones, coming to stand by its arm, and Lena sat. Rhea’s fingers in her hair had her covered in goosebumps. It wasn’t like a few days ago, when she knew nothing and just thought she was cared for; no, now, she knew what those hands had done, and playing along, being the good daughter, made her hate herself more than she ever had before. She clenched her hands into fists to keep them from shaking, or from lashing out and attacking when there was no chance she’d win. 

“There.” Rhea pulled her cowl up, smoothing her hands down over her shoulders. “Beautiful.” 

Mon-El stormed away.

“Stay where you are; we’ll start transmitting in just a moment.”

Lena sat square, deliberately loosening her clenched-shut jaw.

It felt wrong to wear her armor like this. Galaxy Girl was Earth’s, not Daxam’s, and using her - being her - to subjugate the planet and people she was made to protect felt bad, bone-deep.

“You’re doing the right thing.” said Rhea. Even now, her soft voice resonated warmly in Lena, and she hated that she couldn’t shake it. “This planet will finally worship you as the goddess that you are.” 

She kissed Lena’s temple, long fingers curling around her shoulders in a brief embrace, then stepped back. A light flared, and Lena knew she was broadcasting.

“People of National City…” Lena swallowed a lump in her throat, closing her eyes for fortification before beginning again, hands flat in her lap, the shape of the nanobot in her pocket pressing gently up into her palm. “People of National City, I am Galaxy Girl. But you may know me by another name: Lena Luthor.” Lena peeled her cowl off, hands shaking. “I fought alongside National City’s heroes to protect you from those who would do you harm - humans and aliens alike, including the terrorist organization known as Cadmus, run by the woman who adopted me when I was four, Lillian Luthor. But she is not my mother.

“My mother is Queen Rhea of Daxam. We are in the sky above National City right now, and she intends to take control.

“But you can’t let her do that.” Lena swallowed hard, setting her jaw. “You cannot let her have this power over you. Fight back! Fight for your rights, for your families, for your friends and neighbors and heroes. Fight for the Earth. Fight for yourselves.”

“Enough,” Rhea hissed, gripping Lena’s shoulder. “End transmission.”

The man running the broadcast killed it immediately before turning back to Rhea for further instructions. 

“Set up a blockade and arrest any resisters. I don’t want anyone getting in or out of the city.”

He nodded and began to move away, but the communications array lit up. “We’re receiving a communication from Earth.”

Rhea stepped forward, moving between Lena and the holographic panel. “Put it up.”

“Yes, my Lord.”

He waved his hand and then Olivia Marsdin - freaking Olivia Marsdin - flickered into view, with her Edwardian birds’ nest of an updo and an absolutely savage gleam in her eyes. 

“Rhea, Queen of Daxam, my name is President Olivia Marsdin.”

Rhea tilted her head back. “You represent planet Earth?”

“I represent the United States, but today I speak for all humanity when I demand that you abandon your siege of National City.”

“Well, I’d be happy to move my invasion force to Washington, D.C., if you prefer.”

“Oh, I’m not in Washington.” Grimly, the President smiled, leaning in. “I’m heading straight for you.”

Lena barely had to listen out for a moment to hear Air Force One’s engines rumbling closer. 

“National City is mine,” Rhea said, “and you should be thankful that that is all I am currently taking from you.”

“The militaries of Earth will unite against you.”

“I am not afraid of your trembling little militaries.”

“Stand down.”

“‘Stand down?’ I think you are confusing this situation with one in which you have any sort of negotiating leverage.”

“This is not a negotiation. This is a demand.”

“You speak to me like that again and you will feel the consequences - ”

“Oh, my god, enough!” 

Faintly, Lena thought that, if not for the whole kidnapping and invasion scenario, this would be the coolest argument she’s ever had to soak up secondhand panic from.

“Alright, ladies, ladies!” Cat Grant cocked her hip, bracing one hand on it and the other on the lip of the President’s desk. “If I wanted to listen to this adolescent macho posturing, I would have stayed in D.C.”

Lena eyed Rhea - thoroughly engrossed in this war of words. Good.

“Is this really who you want to be? Testosterone-driven windbags, boasting about your big guns? Surely we don’t need to measure anything. We’re women. We’re tough, we’re wise, and we’re way above this pettiness, so let’s just roll up our sleeves and talk peace.”

“I’m sorry,” Rhea said, clearly not sorry in the slightest, “who are you?”

“I’m Cat Grant,” said Cat freaking Grant. “Known on Earth as Queen of All Media.”

“Oh!” Rhea chuckled. “Well, Cat Grant, I’m Rhea, and Earth now has a new Queen.”

“Oh. Oh, well, let me just give you a little bit of friendly advice, Rhea. That tiara that you have on the top of your head, it’s overkill. Real royals, they don’t need to try that hard.”

Rhea bristled with rage, and, silently, Lena stood. As Cat’s precisely barbed parley kept Rhea - and by default, everyone in there - distracted, Lena crept towards the control panel. 

It wasn’t in English, or in Kryptonese, but it was close enough to the latter that she was certain she could figure out how to pilot the ship away. Since the broadcast was between Rhea’s ship and the President’s plane, the other Daxamite ships wouldn’t know not to follow. Most of the ground troops would beam up in time, and the rest - well, she thought, most bullets have at least some lead, and with few enough of them still on Earth, things will go back to normal soon enough. 

“And, the future is female, we’ve all read the t-shirts. So, we are four strong, formidable women - ”

Lena blinked, slipping far enough from the controls that Rhea wouldn’t see her when she turned and looked.

“ - and we can do anything we want. So let’s just talk it out and come up with a harmonious solution, shall we?”

“As I said before, Earth is ours, now.” Rhea wrapped an arm around Lena’s shoulders and pulled her properly into frame. “This planet is her birthright. We don’t confab, we command. This conversation is over.”

With that, the transmission ended, and Rhea fired on Air Force One. 

Lena watched, committing the controls to memory with half her mind as the other half listened out for a familiar sound - Kara’s heartbeat and the whoosh of lower atmospheric wind in her cape. She would save everyone down there, and Lena would finish things off from up here. 

Sure, she’d never see her friends or girlfriend again, but then, they wouldn’t exactly want to see her, now, would they? Not when she was the face of an invasion that threatened to destroy them.

“Do you understand now, l’inah?” Rhea purred, cupping her cheeks, tilting Lena’s head back and peering down at her. “Your choices have consequences for them. I’m surprised that you let this happen.”

Lena pulled away, dropping her chin.

“Then again, they never did give you your dues. All you’ve ever done is help those insignificant little creatures, and not once did they think to worship you as the goddess you are. No wonder you incited them to fight a fruitless battle.” Rhea smiled. “They’ll have all killed themselves before the day is out.” 

“I - ”

“Now. You are to be coronated before the day is out. As much as I’ve enjoyed watching them struggle, there are more important things than making an example of one greasy little stain of a city.”

☆

What was most keenly horrible - not logically, on scales neither grand nor small - was that, under other circumstances, without the logical horror, the big picture and miniature picture horrors, this might have been nice. 

Lena hadn’t ever been the sort of little girl that dreamed of being a princess; her favorite Disney movie growing up was The Rescuers, immediately followed by The Great Mouse Detective. She wore skirts and dresses, in part because they looked nice, but mostly because playing into that particular expectation made shattering others over people’s heads, no matter how far planted up their asses they were, much simpler. 

But, in this unwanted coronation, there seemed to be genuine maternal affection, and a chance to actually do something for Earth. That something, of course, being play goalie from an illusory throne so no one else tried to invade or enslave, then drag New Daxam far off into the emptiest corner of space and succeed in doing to the existing regime what everyone she’s ever loved has done or probably wants to do to her.

Kill.

Who knows how long she’d survive on another planet, since apparently her genetic makeup is as changeable as a radio station - which would also be incredibly cool! as science! under other circumstances! - but at least she’d get to do the one thing she’s actually always wanted: help.

Plenty of things about this could be fascinating. She picked up bits and pieces of Daxam’s language, she was on a space ship, and admittedly, no coronation gown had ever been cooler. Hers fell in line with the same strangely BDSM-based aesthetic of all the other royal garb she’d seen, but in a marginally less overt way, with some elements that she would call Disney foul on if she wasn’t entirely certain that no one on this ship besides her and maybe Mon-El had ever even heard of the mega corporation. 

The boned bodice and the billowy skirt definitely feel like a reference to Kara’s favorite of the princess canon, but there were slits for each of her legs to work through, and she could actually breathe and move without falling out of the neckline. There were strappy sleeves that covered the exact path of her chain-shaped scars and looped down around her fingers, studded with metal cabochons printed with the same crest as her ring, which was now buried in the bottom of her bag. The whole affair was somewhere between the colors of clouds mid-thunderstorm and an old Roman coin, restored and presented under museum lights in a glass case, which was an accurate way to phrase how she felt - trapped and destructive and, somehow, precious.

It was strange, and she didn’t like it one bit. If someone gave her the option, she would have gladly chosen to go back to being an independent and under-appreciated force for good.

She strode back towards her bag - sauntered, really, because it is nigh unto impossible not to saunter when wearing a corset, no matter how tonally inappropriate - and pulled out two things. 

There were, unfortunately, no pockets in her coronation gown, but hey, fabric isn’t made invulnerable by exposure to a yellow sun. She ripped a shallow hole in the lining on the bodice, grabbing a baton and using it to create a hidden zipper, and hid Kara’s note and Jack’s bot in that makeshift pocket. 

Rhea knocked, politely, in a rhythm that she executed with all the familiarity of humans and shave and a haircut. “Are you ready?”

“I - ” Lena stepped into her boots, lacing them with superhuman speed, then stood up and smoothed her hands over her hips. “Zhi.”

“Your pronunciation is impressive, my dear,” Rhea said, opening the door and offering Lena her hand. 

“Khap gaolom, khap azhuhm.”

I become smarter, I become wiser.

“For our people.”

Mouth tight, Lena smiled. “For my people.”

“Our people.” There was a tension in Rhea’s voice, an emphasis, that worried Lena. “There’s this… funny custom on your planet. Political leaders can’t have a hand in private businesses.”

“To help curtail corruption. So someone who works in trading and becomes governor can’t change their state’s trading laws to benefit their company, to the detriment of their constituents.”

“Since you’re going to become regent in just a few short minutes,” Rhea began, looping her arm through Lena’s, “I thought now would be a good time to talk about your private holdings. L Corp.”

It took all of Lena’s bone-deep stubbornness not to flinch. “What about L Corp?”

“I did quite a few things to ensure that I could stay on Earth long enough to bring our people here.” She paused, smiling, squeezing Lena’s elbow fondly. “To bring us closer together. I converted some of my wealth into their currency, I ate their food, I wore their clothes, I spoke their language.”

“Quite well.”

“Daxamites have a gift for languages.” Rhea’s smile grew. “I set up an email at L Corp for internal memos.”

“Did you?”

“I did. And I got one, before we left, offering me something I think I’d quite like to take.”

Goddamnit, Pìa.

“I’m now a member of the L Corp Board of Directors. The exact number doesn’t matter, though apparently, it’s quite high. High enough that, during this… sticky transition, I can use L Corp to ease your way.”

“L Corp has never made anything easy for me,” Lena said, tone deliberately light. 

“Well, it’s about time that changed. Accessing National City’s water supply will be easy enough, though I’ll have to send foot soldiers out into other cities for maximum efficiency - ”

“You’re a chemical engineer - oh, god.”

“And, since I’m your mother, and all your other family is dead, in jail, or on the run, your holdings will revert to me, I’m certain, once you’re coronated.” Rhea laughed, as if anything about this could ever be funny. “No one will be there to stop me, anyway.”

Lena ripped her arm out of Rhea’s grasp. “I have worked too hard to make L Corp a force for good for you to swoop in and use it to drug people so they don’t resist!”

“Oh, it’s just through the transition, dear. Once you’ve taken control of the planet, there won’t be any real way for them to fight your claim.”

“I won’t take control. I won’t do it. If - If I’m not queen of Earth, then I maintain majority ownership of the company, and I’ll veto any attempt you make to drug everyone into submission.” Lena’s eyes burned cold, staring Rhea down flintily as she squared her jaw. “You will never hurt anyone through me ever again.”

Rhea laughed again, this time deeper, darker. She pulled a device out of her pocket, one Lena immediately recognized as a detonator. 

“What are you planning to do with that?”

“One of the things that makes me so proud of you, as a mother, is that you do more with your money and power than live lavishly. You care about the little people.” Rhea inspected the detonator keenly, then looked back up at Lena with eyes as hard and calculating as her own. “The Luthor Family Children’s Hospital is primed to blow at the touch of this button.” Her thumb fluttered over it, and Lena’s heart stopped cold in her chest. 

“Please, don’t.”

“You will rule over New Daxam. The question is, will you agree to the ceremony now, or only after I’ve murdered thousands of the people you’ve sworn to protect? After all, the Luthor’s Children’s Hospital isn’t the only hospital in town.”

“Fine. I will do as you ask.”

Rhea smiled again, all warmth, and put the device away, linking her arm and Lena’s once more and leading her down the hall. “I know it’s hard for you to see now, but in time, you will realize you made the right choice. These… humans, they need to be led. On their backs, we can build to surpass the greatness of Old Daxam. They will construct monuments to our people, to our way of life - to you. Great pyramids like the ones we had back home.”

“Humans already have pyramids,” Lena offered, desperation growing, “built to honor their leaders almost five thousand years ago. They can be great all on their own.”

“Good. We won’t need to teach them how.”

Rhea opened the doors to the throne room, where guards and slaves all stood, waiting. Mon-El was seated on one throne with all the care of someone taking up two seats on a public bus, and he made a great show of not looking Lena’s way when she entered the room. 

Lena swallowed a lump in her throat, remembering everything she’d said to him in the holding cells of the NCPD. Maybe she could start over. Maybe New Daxam could be better. 

Maybe she could do good.

Rhea took her place in the center throne, and Lena knelt, bare knees pressing into the cold, smooth floors, head bowed. 

Because they were speaking to Earth and Daxam, Rhea had conceded that languages from both worlds - both native tongues of their new regent - should be used. She asked Lena every question, first in her own language and then in English, and Lena answered in kind, promising to shepherd two worlds into a golden age of unity under the name of New Daxam. Only rote memorization kept her on task; her eyes were squeezed so tightly shut that she saw colors she hadn’t seen since Maaldoria, holding back tears as she listened with infinite care for Kara’s heart.

It was thunderous, pounding like a war drum. 

She’d never heard Kara sound so angry.

Even so, it was enough to keep her steady through the ceremony, enough to distract her from the faint whine of the broadcast’s electrical signal until a circlet was placed on her head.

It would have been almost weightless to her before she’d developed powers, but somehow, it felt impossibly heavy. It was as if she wore a chain of black holes around her temples, sucking in everything and demolishing it. 

Rhea bid her to stand, and she did, head still drooping. Quietly, she sniffed before lifting her chin and opening her eyes. Staring into the camera, she solemnly swore, “I will do everything in my power to protect you.”

Rhea’s hand on her shoulder gently pushed her down into her throne, and the broadcast stopped. “That was perfect. I am so proud of you.”

Nodding crisply, Lena said, “I think I’d like to go back to my room, for just a moment. If you don’t need me for anything.”

“No, my dear, go take some time to yourself. I’ll send someone for you later.”

“Thank you.”

Lena managed not to run. Somehow, she walked back to her room on the ship with an even stride, slow and measured. Once the doors closed behind her, she sank to the floor in the corner and allowed herself to collapse under the weight of the panic attack that had been waiting in the wings ever since she’d woken up. 

You’re a queen now, she thought with no small degree of bitterness. Live lavishly. Treat yourself. Indulge!

She started to laugh, a horrible, choking sound that she held back with her hands clapped over her mouth, so hard her whole body moved with the force of every chuckle. She wondered what would happen if she found the controller for the genetic dampener in her spine and used it - to overload her brain by ramping her powers up to eleven and shorting it out, keeping it on longer than Rhea had and possibly turning her brain into pudding; to turn herself back into, basically, a human being, but only after she’d thrown herself through the window, and hopefully be impaled on the rooftop spire of some building. 

Part of her actually considered it, too, the part that was too tired to handle all of this but not yet tired enough to just stop moving, to be paralyzed by exhaustion, but that part was far smaller than the part already operating under panic as paralytic, so she just stayed there, wheezing and shaking, fingernails clawing into her cheeks, even when something buzzed.

Things on spaceships don’t usually do that, not in private quarters. Faintly, she hoped it was the start of a slave rebellion, and it was a bomb that would blow her up or pump her full of shards of lead, and then everyone who suffered under the old regime on that ship would escape, join the rebellion on the ground, and together, Daxamites and humans would free themselves from their joint oppressors and everything would be fine once she was dead.

But it wasn’t that. It was too rhythmic, too insistent.

Wow. I even have cell service above skyscrapers! They should put that in their ad campaigns: ‘garbage service whenever you haven’t been abducted and made the figurehead of intergalactic fascism!’

That set her off laughing again, this time shrill and sharp, and her hands came away from her mouth as she slammed her head back into the wall, snatching her off-kilter tiara off her head and throwing it across the room.

“Nice arm you got there, Baudelaire. You play softball in college?”

Lena opened her eyes, prey instincts taking over. 

There, flopping onto the foot of her bed and propping her boots up on the sheets, was the absolute last person Lena would have ever expected to see.

“C’mon,” Livewire said, hopping up and extending her hand to Lena, “it’s only fair I get to rescue your kidnapped ass back.”

Notes for the Chapter:

So. Yeah. Who expected Livewire? I didn't even expect Livewire; or, rather, I didn't expect her to pull this shit. God love a chaotic neutral pseudo-villain who's befriended your hero over gay crushes.

I didn't get to bake, my dad was horrible, and I got next to nothing done.
